In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.5dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This technique's efficacy is substantiated by simulated results which demonstrate its capacity to efficiently handle various types of burst errors. Notably, this approach's effectiveness is validated through actual field trials over the compromised South China Sea cable, enabling data transmission at 72Gbit/s over 18.8km without the debilitating limitations of BER performance. Furthermore, this method's applicability to other fiber links is demonstrated, as it successfully alleviates the spectral distortions in a 10Gbit/s long-haul terrestrial cable prone to burst errors, extending its application to a range of dispersion-spread data-transmission systems. Additionally, this study highlights the crucial role of computational resources in the successful implementation of maximum-likelihood sequence estimation, as it highlights the critical balance between achieving optimal performance and managing the resulting computational complexity. To this end, this study proposes a threshold-based stream-processing strategy, effectively leveraging available computational resources to maximize the transmission rate in practice, ultimately facilitating the practical implementation of this technique in real-world fiber-optic communications systems. By combining this approach with the strategic deployment of digital backplanes with multiple CPUs, this study demonstrates its capacity to efficiently transmit data at up to 100Gbit/s over 10km of underwater cables. Furthermore, this study's findings are applicable to other types of fiber links subject to burst errors resulting from the presence of multiple-spectral-side lobes, as it successfully transmits data at up to 110Gbit/s

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated across three diverse time-series forecasting tasks, yielding an average of 23.75% model parameter reduction, 31.58% fewer multiplications during inference, and a 40.85% increase in model variety without any further optimization. Our code is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/usaio/pruning-in-time. Additionally, we've introduced an overfitting prevention strategy for TCNs, also made available on GitHub at https://github.com/usaio/pruning-in-time/tree/main/anti-quantization-regularization. This approach prevents model growth during the pruning process by incorporating anti-quantization regularization and applying it through the layer-wise technique known as factorized weight pruning. A further optimized variant of this method was entered into the 2021 Time Series Forecasting Challenge, achieving the best reported results at the time on three out of four tasks. Full details of our method and results can be found in our conference paper presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing. Our method has since been recognized as one of the top contributions at the challenge and has inspired the development of time-pruning filters within the Deep Learning4Time series forecasting library. This strategy enables time-pruning variants of multiple TCN layers to be trained in one step using the Pit optimizer, leading to significant gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. Code for this project can be found at https://github.com/usaio/pruning-in-time/tree/main/deep-learning-4-time-series. Furthermore, we've explored the application of our pruning technique to additional Deep Learning models that utilize time- or sequence-based convolutional layers, such as Bidirectional TCNs, Self-Attention networks, and Transformer layers. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in obtaining highly optimized models with reduced parameter counts and inference costs for a range of time-series forecasting

another object. By incorporating 3D coordinates and object attributes into a

and manipulation tasks. Furthermore, our method excels in real-world scenarios

extra data during training. NDFs demonstrate considerable gains in performance
comparative to existing methods. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/robotics-iran/neural-descriptor-fields. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was likely the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -133.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. A [Fe/H] ratio of -1.37 and an [alpha/Fe] ratio of 0.24 were determined for Tononzintla 2, which exhibit typical abundance characteristics of other galactic clusters. A comparison with the Harris catalog cataloged central cluster coordinates within 3 arcminutes and an estimated 8.5 kiloparsec distance to the cluster. A radial velocity model was used to correct for spectroscopic tomography, resolving two close-by and overlapping globular clusters: Tononzintla 2 and CGCG 001-019, which exhibit similar metal content, chemical enrichment patterns, but distinct light curve patterns and estimated 6.5 kiloparsec cluster distance to CGCG 001-019. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. Furthermore, I have undertaken a preliminary analysis of the variables influencing proof length, identifying several significant factors, as well as an exploration of the Isabelle Archive's language use, which reveals that it mirrors patterns observed in natural language, as well as an examination of the effects of different ordering strategies on proof length. This strategy gives priority to proofs with a clear, concise, and varied language use, as well as those characterized by a high degree of internal coherence, as indicated by local clustering coefficients, and a relatively short length. This order is reflected in a new metric that combines multiple variables, paving the way for a more efficient and user-friendly interface for retrieving and interacting with the Isabelle Archive. Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among
electrons within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with
restricted data sets derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron
density functions, the eCPNN model effectively predicts total energies for the
underlying atoms with high precision. Furthermore, when used in place of the
instantaneous potential in the time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger equation, the
eCPNN model successfully predicts spectral frequencies across the spectral range
for the specified atoms. As a result, the eCPNN model offers a promising
electronic structure theory framework that can efficiently and precisely account
for the intricate interelectronic connections in these atomic systems. We have
applied this approach to two-electron density functions and incorporated it
into a novel neural network framework called the Electron Correlation Potential
Neural Network, which can be trained to accurately model various instantaneous
electronic phenomena. We have also demonstrated the utility of this model
in solving linear differential equations that describe time-dependent phenomena,
such as the temporal evolution of electronic densities and spectral frequencies.
We have made the eCPNN code publicly available for further research and
exploration of this promising new approach in physics-inspired deep learning
applications. We have further explored the potential of this model to treat
many-electron systems by examining its performance on full configuration
interaction electron correlation functions for one-dimensional model Hamiltonians,
which suggests that deep learning models can efficiently capture the key
aspects of such correlations. We have also utilized the eCPNN model to
investigate instantaneous electronic localization and bonding patterns in
atomic systems and found that it can provide insights for physics-based
interpretation, thereby demonstrating its value as a tool that complements
traditional quantum chemistry methods. We have expanded the capabilities
of the eCPNN model to treat linear operators and used it to investigate
instantaneous electronic localization and bonding in atomic systems, which
reveals new aspects of electron correlations that cannot be captured by other
density functional theory approaches. We have issued a code for the eCPNN
model that is publicly accessible for exploration and further development. We

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether additional information about the object is used: one group employs object detection methods that integrate pose estimation into their workflow and provide meaningful object descriptions, such as axis representations, for all instances in an image; the other group utilizes object-specific images and projections for reference points or use existing knowledge about the object's structure. However, existing approaches within these categories face notable challenges, including unreliable pose results, particularly when using large training datasets, and the difficulty of estimating poses for certain object categories, such as those with incomplete or complex structures, from limited training data. To address these issues, this research introduces an original framework, DeepHMap++, which first employs a unique projection mapping technique and subsequent group-based method to enhance pose accuracy in comparison to conventional projection methods. The proposed approach is then tested on two large-scale datasets, COFOD and ModelNet4, yielding superior results, especially when using smaller training datasets, thereby demonstrating its capability to estimate full degrees of freedom poses for all objects in an image without the need for axis annotations during training. The code for this research has been made available on the project's official GitHub repository. Furthermore, the paper provides a thorough analysis, including a detailed comparison with state-of-the-art methods, to showcase the effectiveness of DeepHMap++ for full dofs pose estimation on various object categories. Experimental results indicate that DeepHMap++ achieves the best average accuracy of 85.8% on the COFOD dataset and 85.5% on ModelNet4 when using larger training datasets, while notably improving to a record high of 88.5% on COFOD and 87.1% on ModelNet4 when just a single sample is available for each object during training. The model's exceptional performance is attributed to its robust and reliable correspondence learning approach, especially when estimating poses for objects with complex structures or from limited training data. The model's exceptional performance is further evidenced by its low mean and maximum error rates when estimating poses for individual objects and in real-world scenarios. The research paper is currently under review for publication at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023. The model has been found to perform exceptionally well on real-world images, yielding a record low mean and maximum error rates of 0.023 and 0.061, respectively, for all objects in an image when using larger training datasets

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the beam's motion evolves over time. By leveraging the graph's symmetry and the associated spectral properties, we demonstrate the exponential stability of specific eigenmodes. However, counterexamples show that stability can vary greatly across different modes. Moreover, we establish the condition under which all eigenmodes are asymptotically stable. Moreover, we prove that this condition is equivalent to complete controllability in a weaker sense. Counterexamples highlight the importance of the beam's connectivity and the nature of its fixation. The approach involves a nonlocal control mechanism that leverages the elasticity and friction within the graph. The method's effectiveness is illustrated through the achievement of robust stability. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This algorithm first solves the centrality calculations for each layer as if they were individual networks, then combines the results to produce a more accurate solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a co-author network and a network of city collaborations. Our results show that our method outperforms existing multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks in terms of solution convergence and precision. Furthermore, our method can be used with any network layer configuration, making it a versatile and useful tool for multi-layer network analysis. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes, marking the end of surface seal, have been widely debated but lacking in this research is a detailed analysis of the underlying dynamics that govern this intermediate speed surface seal regime. Through high-speed camera recordings and resulting fluid simulations, our work reveals the crucial role of velocity, sphere size, and surrounding water pressure in this intermediate surface seal regime. It is shown that at high speeds, the splash dome closure is initiated by the sphere's downward movement, while at lower speeds, water pressure plays a more significant part. A theoretical framework, incorporating inelastic collisions and fluid pressure effects, is also developed to predict when surface seal ends in the intermediate speed regime. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the water entry surface seal behavior, including the formation of the splash dome, for spheres impacting the water's surface at intermediate speeds. The study's findings can also be applied to other objects entering water at these velocity ranges, contributing to a broader understanding of the surface seal phenomenon. The research focuses on the surface seal regime characterized by a distinct splash dome formation, differentiating it from another water entry behavior known as ventus, which forms bubbles within the water. The work's advancements on the surface seal front, specifically the intermediate speed regime, may also provide insights into optimizing the performance of water-based transportation systems by minimizing drag caused by surface seal. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. Consequently, the $\theta$-terms destroy universal symmetries in an infinite range of the spectrum, rendering it ineffective in the low-energy range. Moreover, we found that the $\theta$-terms may also destroy some universal symmetries in the vacuum, yielding a potential explanation for the cosmological constant problem. Finally, we examined the potential for the R-R sector to be replaced with an algebraic lattice of scalar field directions, avoiding the violation of supersymmetry. This replacement would necessitate the addition of a potential $\theta$-term related to the graviphoton, destroying any residual universal symmetries that may persist after considering charged states. Ultimately, all directions of the moduli space must be effectively described by an effective field theory. The requirements for this effectiveness may give rise to an upper limit on the scale of such Type IIB theories. The implication of this study on the study of quantum gravity at high energies, beyond the reach of the Planck scale, also is discussed. Mobile device owners frequently require running security-risky apps for entertainment or necessity, but are hesitant to grant these apps access to sensitive inputs like biometrics and cameras due to trust issues. 

In evaluating what hardware to isolate for secure apps, several factors need to be balanced:

* The amount of trust in the OS, which dictates the isolation's effectiveness
* The performance impact of creating isolated environments
* Hardware costs and the resulting thermal management issues

Our research reveals the optimal approach to achieving the best balance between trust and performance at minimal additional hardware cost. 

In particular, we found that for the majority of apps tested, assigning an isolated hardware segment that is not shared with the OS (user-space) resulted in a noticeable decrease in trust, but only a slight performance improvement. 

However, this approach comes with a significant increase in hardware costs. 

On the other hand, assigning an isolated hardware segment that is shared with the OS (kernel-space) offered little improvement in trust but resulted in a significant decrease in performance. 

However, this approach also increased hardware costs, although to a certain extent. 

In contrast, assigning an isolated hardware segment that is shared with the OS but with some overlap resulted in the best balance between trust and performance, with only a slight increase in hardware costs. 

This research provides a reference for evaluating the performance and security of various hardware isolation strategies. 

In addition, our findings can be applied to the design of hardware policies that manage the sharing of hardware resources between apps, as well as to the development of system configurations that can efficiently manage hardware resources. 

Our research also offers insights that can be used to optimize the performance of secure-computation frameworks that rely on hardware isolation. 

Our research utilized a range of apps with diverse security profiles and different hardware platforms, ensuring the broadest possible applicability of our findings. 

Our research demonstrated that the optimal approach to hardware isolation can vary greatly depending on the app, with some apps requiring strong OS trust, while others can function effectively with minimal OS trust.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously studied methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control domains. Our research contributes a comprehensive framework for analyzing robust reinforcement learning. The proposed FPG algorithm is a robust reinforcement learning framework providing an optimal policy robust to strong data corruption. FPG is an adaptable framework that can be optimized using a variety of optimization techniques, such as minimizing the corruption's loss. We discovered a key property that the expected corrupted transition probabilities equals the sum of transition probabilities for each corruption. This property enables the filtering of corrupted transitions by distinct filters. We leveraged these filters to design a robust loss function that is the negative sum of the expected returns for all filters. The proposed FPG algorithm is an example of how to implement this robust loss function using reinforcement learning. We're examining the band structure of a honeycomb lattice, consisting of two interlocking Moir\'e patterns, within the $\mathbf{k}$-space, specifically within the irreducible representations of the wallpaper group.  Our primary concern lies with the creation of zero-energy points, known as Dirac points, and our findings indicate that these points can be engineered through an external potential, serving as a tunable feature.  We demonstrate that certain Dirac points within the interior of the irreducible zone remain isolated and stable even with the introduction of long-range hoppings.  We also illustrate the modification induced by an external potential on the lattice, resulting in the shifting of Dirac points to rational incommensurate positions within the irreducible zone.  To overcome sampling error risks, we employ the spectral representation method, relying on spectral functions rather than lattice models.  This study is relevant to recent graphene-silica superstructure research, where isolated Dirac points have been observed and our results suggest that these points could resist topological perturbations, making them robust.  Finally, we discuss the potential for these points to be probed experimentally using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.  We also explore strategies for modifying Dirac points through different types of symmetry-breaking potentials, potentially leading to mass acquisition and associated fermionic Fermi pockets.  Ultimately, this work contributes to the broader understanding of topological electronic properties in weakly coupled systems.  Additionally, we examine how discrete symmetry influences the quasi-periodic lattice model, emphasizing the distinction between commensurate and incommensurate symmetry operations, as well as the implications for our results, and we outline potential paths for experimental validation using graphene-silica superstructures, graphene-hexagonal BN superstructures, and BN-silica superstructures.  Finally, we outline two potential routes for further theoretical investigation: analyzing the discrete symmetry effects on flat bands within 1D and 3D quasi-periodic systems and exploring the generalization of our findings to more complex electronic structures.  As such, this work provides a foundation for delving into the discrete symmetry effects on topological electronic properties in quasi-periodic systems.  Ultimately, we anticipate that our results will inspire further theoretical and experimental exploration of weakly coupled systems, unlocking a deeper understanding of the interplay between symmetry, electronic structure, and strong correlations in these complex systems. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our proposed solution employed direct transcription using the Newton method and specified appropriate penalties for estimation and control objectives. Our results compared different Runge-Kutta orders, with a focus on potential applications during the pandemic when manufacturing capacity was limited, suggesting a high-order method such as RK7M8 for its efficient computation time and robust performance. We also examine alternative approaches and potential improvements to the method, specifically the potential benefits of using nonlinear filters, different transcription and resolution techniques, and modifying air flow resistance, with a focus on potential applications during the pandemic when manufacturing capacity was limited. Our results, however, indicate that manufacturing modifications were not necessary, rendering further investigation on those fronts less urgent in the short term. Furthermore, we explore potential extensions of this research to other applications, specifically those involving the estimation of parameters in continuous systems with the potential for abrupt changes, and the development of robust controllers against unforeseen component failures. Our proposed solution and case study provide a comprehensive introduction to direct transcription methods, while an accompanying supplementary material offers detailed derivations, additional results, and a comprehensive list of employed MATLAB codes and packages for easy replication and extension. Additionally, we include a brief overview of the ventilator shortage issue during the COVID-19 pandemic, along with a brief examination of our results in the context of this crisis. Our study and the broader issue of ventilator shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic serve as a prime example of the kind of complex estimation and control challenges that need to be addressed in the healthcare sector, with our proposed solution offering a comprehensive solution to the dual-patient ventilation problem, while also highlighting the urgent need for further research on robust continuous state estimation and control in the face of uncertainty. We introduce a novel approach for automatically isolating tumors in the esophagus from CT scans, a challenging task due to low contrast and the varied presence of surrounding organs. To improve accuracy, our solution, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), leverages advanced neural network components, including dense blocks and attention mechanisms, which are uncommon in prior esophageal tumor segmentation studies. We further customize DDAUnet to accommodate incomplete and organ-overlapping CT scans by adding boundary padding and a multi-organ mask pre-processing step. Thorough evaluations using two public datasets (Cader and Li) validate our method's effectiveness, with DDAUnet outperforming existing competitors. Notably, our approach excels in processing scans with incomplete organ cross-sections. The code is openly available for research reference. Furthermore, a user-friendly, openly accessible software for automatic tumor segmentation has been developed and is hosted on an online repository. The software's primary components include DDAUnet and 3D visualization tools. The openly accessible code and software allow for replication of results and potential adaptation in clinical settings. The model's performance accuracy serves as a basis for potential clinical applications, including cancer measurement and treatment planning. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites often contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. However, the accuracy of such interpretations relies on the skills of their interpreters. Furthermore, the data used for geosteering also includes noisy measurements from the well logs, which further complicates the interpretation by introducing uncertainty. This research aims to automate the formation evaluation process in real-time by combining multiple interpretations generated through a semi-analytical model, using data from well logs. This approach, tested on synthetic logs, yielded a high correlation (.99) between the original and estimated values. Additionally, the variation in the results highlighted the influence of uncertainty on the well logging tools. Furthermore, this approach demonstrated its applicability to complex formations and logging tools with high noise levels. As a practical application, this research was utilized to guide the real-time geosteering of development wells in a mature oil field in the Middle East. The results showed that the approach is effective in reducing the time and cost associated with drilling by avoiding unexpected formations and minimizing the need for logging tool changes. Overall, this research provides a method for accurately interpreting well logs in real-time, prioritizing efficiency and effectiveness over detailed layer-by-layer analyses. This approach is now being utilized by the company in other oil fields. As the industry continues to shift towards digital technologies, this research is an important step in the development of advanced geosteering tools. This paper provides a detailed overview of the approach, including the challenges it overcomes and its benefits. Furthermore, it highlights the results obtained when the method was applied to real-world scenarios. This research is now being further developed to accommodate electrical logging, which is increasingly being utilized in the industry. This extension is expected to yield equal or better performance metrics. This is the second paper on this subject, with the first paper being presented at the 2018 SPE Europec Conference. This paper is an expanded version of the previous paper, with additional details and data. This research is ongoing, with the company continuing to collaborate with the research institution. This collaboration has resulted in the development of multiple patents and innovative technologies. This research institution is a leading center for research and innovation in the industry, with a strong focus on digital technologies and geophysics. This company is one of the leading operators in the industry, with a diverse portfolio of oil and gas projects globally.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a key extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve and analyze text-based information. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our method exhibits superior extensional performance when scaling to larger corpora. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/ASAI-THU/Nested-NER. For the English dataset, our results match the existing literature, hence we did not include them in the code. For the Chinese dataset, models and codes are included in the package. Moreover, this study is the first to introduce the Chinese Public Entity Dictionary (Cped) at https://github.com/ASAI-THU/Cped, which can be applied to various NER tasks requiring a dictionary. Cped uses the same data structure as the widely adopted CoNLL-2003 format and includes 20 categories for entity annotation. We hope our proposed holistic modeling can guide the community toward more sophisticated and effective nested NER techniques. Furthermore, we believe that our issued multi-task challenge trials can spur breakthroughs in both NER and machine translation. Our challenge and the models' codes are available at https://github.com/ASAI-THU/Nested-NER-Challenge. Our proposed challenge is the first multi-task challenge that combines NER and machine translation, with the aim of evaluating the ability of models to extract information from input texts. We introduce a new evaluation metric called BERT-based NER NLU NLP Score (B4N4S), which combines the standard F1 score with the BERT-based NLU score. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a notable reduction in location-related mistakes. Furthermore, our solution facilitates real-world implementation and does not require intricate mathematical concepts. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by conducting extensive, randomized trials within a controlled environment and report the precise parameters of our simulation setup. Ultimately, our approach achieves an accurate location estimation of less than a metre on average. We have also examined the impact of key variables on location estimation and observed the behavior of our method in response to these factors. Interestingly, our results reveal that, in certain situations, location estimation can be as precise as 0.5 metres. We discuss potential applications and areas for further development, as well as potential avenues for exploration in the broader field of location detection within networks. Ultimately, our solution is adaptable to location detection in any wireless communication technology that relies on signal strength to determine distance. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By highlighting existing challenges and future opportunities, we aim to spark discussion among the NLP community regarding code-mixing research, encourage collaboration, and facilitate access to code-mixing resources for all stakeholders. Furthermore, we introduce an open-access, multilingual Code-Mixing Corpus Annotation Guide to standardize the marking of code-mixing data, ensuring consistency and facilitating comparison of different code-mixing studies. By standardizing annotation practices and promoting code-mixing research, we can develop more effective and practical NLP solutions for real-world applications within multilingual societies. This initiative can also benefit other underrepresented topics and domains by outlining a similar research framework and providing a useful reference for future work. This paper is an invitation to the NLP community to engage with code-mixing research, address existing challenges, and explore new opportunities for developing more practical and adaptable NLP solutions. This knowledge can be adapted to other code-mixing language combinations, and researchers, in turn, can benefit from the consideration of challenges and considerations in the NLP domain. This is especially relevant to multilingual communities where different languages coexist, and there is considerable interest in developing more effective NLP tools to support daily life, particularly for those with limited resources and significant disparities in the global digital society. This research is also relevant to multilingual individuals with distinct proficiency levels, different first languages, and those with varying levels of literacy, offering a more comprehensive understanding of code-mixing research in the NLP domain. We analyzed user locations and misinformation sharing on Reddit in the US and found a strong correlation between users' geographic proximity and misinformation dissemination between them. This phenomenon, dubbed the "Big Geographic Sort," significantly explains variations in misinformation dissemination among regions, accounting for up to 73% of regional differences. We observed regional misinformation dissemination patterns persist even when controlling for factors like population size, education levels, and internet penetration, suggesting that the Big Geographic Sort plays a crucial role. Moreover, we identified age as an important moderator, with older adults exhibiting higher regional variability in misinformation dissemination. We based our methods on online anonymization practices and obtained datasets from Reddit through publicly available APIs. The findings suggest that the Big Geographic Sort contributes substantially to online misinformation dissemination and highlight the importance of considering spatial factors in information dissemination models. Ultimately, recognizing these regional patterns is essential for developing targeted strategies to combat the dissemination of misinformation. We propose evaluating the effectiveness of misinformation dissemination interventions by analyzing changes in regional misinformation dissemination patterns. Furthermore, we suggest that mitigating the Big Geographic Sort could be an essential component of such assessments. We found that reducing regional variability in misinformation dissemination does not necessarily translate to decreased overall dissemination rates. Therefore, developers and researchers of online platforms should be aware of the potential unintended consequences of interventions aimed at mitigating the Big Geographic Sort. The underlying forces driving the Big Geographic Sort, such as socioeconomic factors and online platform design, warrant further exploration and analysis. Building on previous work, we propose an algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of possible node connections. The proposed method utilizes a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials to determine the degree of each node, allowing for the flexible creation of rooted trees with varying degrees. We demonstrate that this approach produces trees that conform to a specific distribution, characterized by the probability distributions of their degree sequences. Furthermore, we show that our algorithm is efficient, producing results that are statistically comparable to those from established methods for a significant sample size. We explore the accuracy of our algorithm by analyzing its components and confirming that they are mutually independent. Our analysis provides insight into the degree sequence distribution and we confirm that it complies with the fundamental properties of degree sequences. We also examine the algorithm's performance, noting that the choice of degree sequence distribution impacts tree generation. We investigate two specific degree sequence distributions, one following an autoregressive process and another corresponding to a specific stationary distribution. Our results are relevant to the study of tree-valued stochastic processes, such as the Brownian tree model, and our analysis highlights the importance of the degree sequence distribution of the underlying tree process. Our work also lays the groundwork for further investigation into the properties of tree-valued processes, with a focus on the degree sequence distribution. By correlating the magnification with the redshift of foreground galaxies, we've calculated a lensing signal in a region of redshift space where systematic errors are minimized. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. The implementation of photonic technology in SOI devices helps enhance photon collection efficiency, allowing for the observation of spin-dependent optical transitions in T centers even when they are deeply buried. Initial results with these defect centers in SOI have shown that it may be possible to achieve a key requirement for quantum communication - the ability to execute precise control over the interaction between spins and photons - potentially paving the way for the development of robust quantum communication systems. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of T centers in SOI may also enable the development of secure optical communication systems that do not require the reversal of bulk silicon fabrication processes used previously. Building on these breakthroughs, future research will focus on refining the creation of these defect centers through optimized fabrication processes, as well as the development of efficient and precise techniques for controlling the interaction between spins and photons. Overall, it appears that T centers in SOI have significant potential to contribute to the creation of robust and controllable quantum communication systems. Ultimately, achieving this goal will depend on the outcome of ongoing and future research aimed at enhancing the efficiency and controllability of these defect centers. As such, it is essential that this work remains open-access to ensure the free exchange of ideas between researchers in this field. In this research, we explore the properties of degenerate Bernoulli polynomials and degenerate umbral operators to demonstrate the equivalences between degenerate Bernoulli polynomials, degenerate umbral operators, and the binomial expansion formula. Furthermore, we derive the coefficients of the degenerate umbral operator and the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial using the algebraic approach, and we introduce a new degenerate umbral operator based on the coefficients. This new operator is shown to generate the classical and geometric degenerate Bernoulli polynomials. Additionally, we establish the relationship between the degenerate umbral operator and the degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind, resulting in closed-form expressions for the degenerate Stirling numbers. This research expands on prior works by Carlitz, Roush, and Mortenson in the context of degenerate umbral calculus. Lastly, we conclude this study by outlining potential future investigations in the field.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, specifically those generated by word2vec, are affected by the classification of Loughran-McDonald's sentiment labels on financial news articles. Our analysis utilizes mathematical concepts, such as distributional inferences and relative distribution inferences, to gain insight into the structure of the word embeddings and their relation to the sentiment labels. Through empirical studies and simulations, we explore the degree to which the word embeddings align with the sentiment labels and propose a new metric, called the relative distribution inference precision, to evaluate the accuracy of the word embeddings. Our research reveals that the skip-gram model can capture the classification of sentiment labels on basic parts of language, such as nouns and verbs, but its effectiveness decreases for more complex aspects like relationships and groups. Furthermore, we discover that the accuracy of the word embeddings depends on the distance between the classification of the target word and the classification of the surrounding words in the training corpus. Our analysis demonstrates that the structure of the word embeddings is more precise when the skip-gram model is trained with a large and diverse sampling of the corpus's content. Additionally, we explore the applicability of our analysis to other types of word embeddings, such as the global vector for word marriage model, and the challenges and opportunities presented by our research. Through our findings, we demonstrate the value of mathematically examining the internal structure of word embeddings and the potential for cross-fertilization between machine learning and mathematics in the study of these models. Our work is also significant from a practical standpoint, providing a clear framework for the evaluation of word embeddings in the context of the classification of financial text. Finally, we explore the scope for further research into the underlying structure of word embeddings and their reliance on the classification of the training corpus's content. Additionally, we highlight the importance of open-source repositories of pre-trained models that have been trained on diverse datasets, to facilitate the exploration of these models' underlying structures and the development of more advanced versions. Our study is relevant to the broader NLP community, with implications for the use of word embeddings in the analysis of text data and the development of models that can provide a more accurate and robust understanding of language. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, a consistent and efficient numerical method has been developed for solving solidification and melting problems. The method utilizes a level-set interface representation and the embedded boundary method for numerical integration, leveraging the former's flexibility in tracking complex and dynamic interface shapes and the latter's ability to handle irregular boundary calculations. A primary advantage of this method is its ability to handle melting scenarios where changes in phase lead to significant changes in density and heat transfer properties at the interface. A numerical validation of the method is provided by examining a range of test cases, including the solidification of a concentrated dye, a phase change with convection, and a layer melting due to an external heat source. The study shows that the method produces accurate results when compared to established models, demonstrating its effectiveness for a variety of changing phase scenarios, including both solid-to-solid and solid-to-fluid phase transitions. The research also analyzes the method's performance in terms of numerical efficiency and error behavior, providing a detailed numerical analysis of different variational integrals and the method's adaptability for high-performance computing. The study finds that the method yields reliable and consistent results for a broad range of scenarios and grid sizes, and the development of the method is suitable for implementation on distributed computing systems. The research is an extension of earlier work on the method, with the new results showing the method's capability for solving a broader range of changing phase problems. To rectify this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. Furthermore, the proposed approach facilitates an extension of the directionally based coherence space model, integrating the categorial inference capability of the Lambek Calculus. Our method's applicability and effectiveness are demonstrated through the exploration of a previously analyzed example with lexical and derivational ambiguity. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the best known results to date. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the polynomial guarantees it establishes. This research provides the groundwork for exploring more demanding objectives, such as ensuring positive payoff accumulation or maximizing the minimum payoff, casting them as approximate rationalizability challenges. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We also explore various parametrization-independent properties of these surfaces, including their growth and the distribution of their looptraits. Additionally, we provide an appendix detailing the convergence of multiple SLE in time within the upper half-plane. This analysis builds on previous research by the same authors with Miller and Sheffield. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts MediaWiki into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts. Developed by the ASPIRE Center, WorkingWiki enables a versatile authoring environment for various document types, including books, research papers, and conference proceedings. With features tailored to enhance research collaboration, WorkingWiki boasts a user-friendly interface and intuitive tools for managing content, collaborating with others, and tracking progress. Its capabilities include real-time co-authoring, grammar and spell checking, a built-in citation manager, and a modular layout system. Furthermore, WorkingWiki integrates sophisticated validation tools, a reliable version control system, and a secure and private data storage mechanism. By integrating multiple open-source tools and utilizing MediaWiki's robust framework, WorkingWiki offers a free and user-friendly alternative to paid authoring platforms. Its source code is available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. Furthermore, the ASPIRE Center offers customized WorkingWiki instances to research groups through a simple subscription-based model. With the rise of remote work and collaboration, WorkingWiki is an ideal solution for managing research projects and ensuring data security and integrity. Unlike traditional cloud-based services, WorkingWiki provides full control over data by storing it on a local server. With WorkingWiki, researchers can leverage a versatile authoring environment to produce high-quality manuscripts, combining the functionality of typesetters, style guides, and collaboration tools into a single, integrated platform. By utilizing WorkingWiki, researchers can produce manuscripts in various formats, including LaTeX, MS Word, and HTML. Additionally, WorkingWiki generates validation reports, version control records, and metadata summaries that facilitate the manuscript submission process. With its robust features and collaborative approach, WorkingWiki is an innovative tool that revolutionizes the research writing process, providing a seamless and efficient experience for authors, making it an ideal solution for any research project. WorkingWiki is available at https://workingwiki.org. Its source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ASPIRE-Center/WorkingWiki. We present a novel universal method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior,
including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of
coherence. This method automatically identifies and differentiates between synchronized
clusters, traveling wave patterns, chimera states, and asynchronous states. Additionally,
it is capable of determining the number of clusters present in cluster synchronization
situations. To further enhance our method, we developed a new technique for measuring the
speed of traveling chimera states. We demonstrate and validate our method using a
specific example of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with asymmetric
nonlocal inhibitory connections, where a variety of coherent and incoherent states occur
depending on the initial conditions. Our proposed method offers a straightforward solution
for identifying the complex behavior observed in multichannel phase space plots without the
need for further dimensionality reduction. We make available our developed code for the
freely accessible xpylobby framework, along with an accompanying tutorial for users to
replicate our results. Moreover, we provide a detailed analysis of our method's execution
time and memory usage for broad applicability. Our research offers a universal solution
for the coherent cluster identification problem and can be applied across various networks
consisting of nonlinear neurons with nonlocal interactions. Furthermore, we explore the
robustness of our method by examining its performance in the presence of noisy neuron behavior. 
Our results show that our method remains effective even with high levels of external noise. 
We explore the effects of different connection strengths and discover that our method is
primarily driven by the coherence within local neighborhoods. Finally, we investigate the
effects of different initial conditions and demonstrate that our method is accurate across
a wide range of starting points. Our research provides a groundbreaking approach for the
universal detection of traveling chimera and synchronized cluster states in complex
spiking networks using a simple and robust method. This breakthrough is expected to
significantly contribute to the advancement of nonlinear dynamics research and the discovery
of novel cluster states in complex networks. Additionally, this method is expected to be
applied across a wide range of fields that study the complex behavior of spiking networks in
biology, physiology, and other related domains. Furthermore, this research is also
expected to facilitate the development of new medication treatments for neurological
disorders such as epilepsy by providing a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms
of wave patterns and cluster states. This is the first study that offers a universal
solution for the coherent cluster identification problem

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' variability, a consistent underlying approach has yet to be identified. We propose the Remove-Win design framework to capture unifying principles of update resolution, leveraging "win" and "remove" operations to design CRDTs that can handle multiple changes at once. By providing a general design framework and illustrative examples such as multi-sets and CRDT counters, we aim to provide insight into the design of CRDTs through the lens of "win" and "remove" updates. Additionally, the framework is applied to design novel CRDTs for multi-sets and counter collections with strong consistency guarantees. The implementation of the proposed designs in terms of latency and throughput is also examined, showing that the Remove-Win framework is effective in designing high-performance CRDTs. The framework is an initial exploration into the design of CRDTs, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through the design of multiple existing and novel CRDTs. Furthermore, the framework is used to identify potential flaws in existing replication approaches, such as the anti-entropy protocol, highlighting the importance of considering the win-remove framework's fundamental design principles. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. In addition, by analyzing protein products in relation to each other, we have discovered new traits associated with recombination rates, expression levels, chromatin states and other genomics characteristics and importantly, our approach is highly adaptable for the analysis of additional genome-wide association studies of human traits. Our comprehensive data sets are available at http://www.1000genomes.org/wiki/Category:Tabbed_content:Functional_prediction and in supplementary materials. In conclusion, our study has shed light on how genomic elements influence specific traits and their production, expression and function. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre suggest their brightness remains relatively stable, implying an underlying process with significant power. To explain this, researchers consider the possibility of these sources to feature an accretion disc that is periodically filled with a specific amount of material. To make progress in understanding these sources, studies have been conducted on another type of variable X-ray binaries - those that originate from the merger of a neutron star and a companion star. These neutron star binaries can form an accretion disc if the star passes through a certain phase of its life, but it will only do so intermittently. By examining how frequently a neutron star accretes, along with other characteristics of the binary system, a new approach is being explored to determine the total number of seconds these systems have been operating. Additionally, by linking this to the overall duration of the binary's operation, a new indicator of the nature of the Galactic Centre's variable X-ray sources has been created. Based on observations of these neutron star binaries at a distance from the Earth, a pattern has been identified - a specific time frame is followed by a significantly longer period of activity, and this pattern is followed by an extended period where the source is inactive. By comparing this to the Earth's orbit around the Sun, this time frame of activity is found to be equivalent to the time it takes a neutron star to orbit its companion star, while the longer period of activity is equivalent to the time it takes the neutron star to orbit the Sun, although this is much longer than the Earth's orbital time. Using this new approach and data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, the time frame of activity has been determined for five of these neutron star binaries, and their duration of operation has been estimated to be anywhere between 10 to 30 days. Based on these findings, a new explanation is given for the relatively stable brightness of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre, suggesting that these sources are not powered by the continuous accumulation of material, but rather the recurrence time of their binary systems. A/ASCA data on these sources have also been analyzed, and while no evidence of an X-ray luminosity that varies with the neutron star's spin was found, it is possible that such a relationship could exist if the neutron star's spin is relatively slow. Finally, by considering the possibility that some of these variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre are powered by the same type of binary systems that produce gamma-ray bursts, a new explanation is given for the nature of these sources

It has been proven that any classical or welded knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of diagonal moves and Reidemeister moves. Moreover, it can be shown that a specific variation of the diagonal move can be employed in welded knots, allowing for an unknotted loop to pass through another loop without the need for crossing changes. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. Lastly, we demonstrate that this hypersurface undergoes a process of splitting at the value of r equal to 1 and is therefore not compact. Additionally, we prove that it is subject to a process of pinching and ultimately collapses to a flat torus defined by the union of two circles with equal radii. This occurs under specific linear transformations, known as the umbral technique, with a standard hypersurface with a radius of 1. Next-generation cardiac surgical interventions demand precise preoperative planning to minimize post-surgical complications and mortality rates. Advances in cardiac imaging and deep learning are providing new possibilities for treating congenital heart defects. However, there is a significant lack of large-scale cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) datasets containing rare defects, hindering the training of accurate and generalizable segmentation models. Existing studies primarily focus on common defects, accounting for less than 50% of total congenital heart disease cases. In this study, we assess the generalizability of a UNet-based segmentation model trained on the ACDC dataset, which contains data for several common cardiac conditions but lacks information on rare defects, such as total anomalous pulmonary venous connection, partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection, and cor triatriatum. The model demonstrates high accuracy in segmenting left and right ventricles, the myocardium, and the left and right walls but fails to achieve the same level of performance on more complex structures like the atria. When applied to CMRI images of rare congenital heart diseases, the model exhibits significantly inferior performance, with a mean absolute surface difference of 9.6 for the left ventricle, 11.9 for the right ventricle, 12.9 for the left wall, and 15.1 for the right wall. These findings highlight the need for large-scale datasets containing a wide range of cardiac abnormalities to ensure accurate preoperative planning. Until then, surgical teams may need to rely on other imaging modalities, such as computed tomography or cardiac catheterization, which provide structural information essential for safe cardiac interventions. Furthermore, the incorporation of multi-structure UNet variants, like the one employed in this study, may offer a more comprehensive understanding of cardiac anatomy and a more secure foundation for future preoperative planning systems. In recognition of the limitations and exclusive focus on CMRI, our research is dedicated to Rui Zhang, the primary user who contributed greatly to our discussions. In addition, we express our gratitude to Dr. Rui Zhang for allowing us to utilize his name in this tribute. The considered functionals embody a specific type of static model that quantifies damage in heterogeneous materials. The model's ultimate behavior is comprehensively defined by Gamma-convergence based on the relative rates at which its approximations and oscillation parameters converge. The research is particularly focused on analyzing the impact of macroscopic integration when modeling materials with significantly disparate components. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Code is available at: https://github.com/youshen1990/FPN-Fusion. Overall, the proposed methods deliver superior performance with simpler designs, outperforming previous FPN variants by a significant margin. Furthermore, recommended best practices for designing pyramidal backpropagation pathways can be applied across various detection frameworks, yielding improved results. Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. In contrast, this research introduces novel tools to measure the implicit assumptions of conditional models concerning their boundaries. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme cases of a specific type of model, including the distribution of a tail event and a key metric of asymptotic independence. The method is then demonstrated with a widely used model, and an alternative condition is also introduced to address limitations in the original Heffernan-Tawn model, particularly regarding its inability to capture certain cases of asymptotic independence. Furthermore, this research introduces an alternative condition to address these limitations, yielding results that can be applied across a broader range of models, including those with non-standard forms. In addition, an important aspect of this condition is that it can be applied in an unconditional setting, providing a valuable extension to existing methods. In conclusion, this research offers a significant advancement in the evaluation and comparison of conditionally specified models, particularly in regards to their extreme behavior. Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of choosing correlated orbitals and constructing Wannier functions within the DFT framework. Despite variations in the DFT implementation, our study shows that using a consistent set of correlated orbitals and Wannier functions yields consistent results. We focus on the complex hybridizations occurring between 3d $p$ and $d$ states and demonstrate that, within a DFT+DMFT framework, these complex interactions must be accurately represented to capture the underlying physics. We examine the need for a more intricate hybridization diagram, often overlooked in such models, and provide evidence that, in SrMnO$_3$, it significantly affects the outcome of the calculation, particularly when attempting to replicate experimental results for this material. We establish that, in order to replicate the expected atomic physics, it is essential to solve the DMFT problem on the real-frequency axis, rather than employing a lattice of effective impurities. We also highlight the importance of incorporating both $p$-$d$ and $d$-$d$ complex hybridizations within the Wannier function set, in order to capture the detailed magnetic and lattice distortions within this compound. Ultimately, our findings suggest that, in order to create a consistent and accurate DFT+DMFT framework for modeling 3d transition-metal oxides, it is essential to consider the intricate hybridizations present within these materials. As such, this approach holds significant potential for further exploration into the physics of these complex systems. In a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, typically used for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum, a notable spectral shift around anomalies occurs. This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer. However, this analysis fails to account for the gyroscope's frame of reference. To address this oversight, we employ a 4-vector approach and derive a long-wavelength limit for the spectral shift, demonstrating that the shift's direction reverses when the gyroscope transitions from a rotating state to a state at rest with respect to an observer. Notably, this reversal occurs precisely at the critical angular velocity $\omega_c$ that marks the onset of spectral shift anomalies, as identified by Leonhardt and Philippi, at $\omega_c \approx 3.19 \omega_L$. Moreover, we demonstrate that the spectral shift anomalies arise due to the distinction between co- and counter-propagating components of the light field within the Sagnac interferometer, leading to a spectral shift switch anomalies at $\omega_c$. The proposed spectral shift switch anomalies provide a novel explanation for the spectral shift patterns observed in previous studies. The theoretical framework presented can be applied to design novel sensing mechanisms by engineering spectral shift switch anomalies in Sagnac interferometer and its derivatives. The spectral shift switch anomalies and the associated spectral shift patterns may also be observed with a gyroscope at a much slower rotation rate than what is typically required for calibration purposes. The proposed concept of spectral shift switch anomalies can be extended to other gyroscopic phenomena, such as gyroscope-based detection of chiral symmetry breaking, offering a novel approach to the study of these phenomena. The theoretical framework can be experimentally verified by conducting a gyroscope-based investigation of spectral shift switch anomalies in the presence of a parametric perturbation. The proposed experiment can be performed using a rotating gyroscope in a vacuum environment, such as in a gyroscope-based setup in a satellite in orbit around the Earth. The experimental verification of the proposed concept can provide a deeper understanding of the underlying physics of spectral shift switch anomalies, while the proposed experiment can contribute to the development of novel sensing mechanisms and the study of chiral symmetry breaking in gyroscopes. The theoretical framework can be applied to design novel gyroscopic sensors based on the principle of spectral shift switch anomalies, such as a gyroscope-based sensor for detecting symmetry breaking in circularly polarized light, such as in the case of a rotating gyroscope in a vacuum
