A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this foundation, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the government. Moreover, we introduce 'credibility' as a secondary concept to describe actions that, although not necessarily demonstrating the passcode's correctness, do so implicitly. We delve into the intricacies of both demonstrability and credibility, as well as 'coercibility', which refers to the potential for the government to compel the respondent to incriminate themselves. We examine both a'strong' and 'weak' coercibility standard. We also explore the implications of our framework on compelled actions such as speaking, writing, and physical actions like entering a passcode or biometric identification. Ultimately, we conclude that compelling a user to enter their passcode is analogous to compelling that user to acknowledge a written statement by signing their name, and that both fall under the category of actions that are both demonstrable, credible, and coercible. Furthermore, we contend that our framework offers a useful perspective on the long-standing case of Jaggard v. Edwards, as well as the more recent case of United States v. Davis. We also examine the reach of our framework on other compelled actions like speech, writing, and biometric identification, and we explore the implications of our framework on the broader topic of compelled production. We use our framework to analyze and provide insight into a novel scenario, as well as into existing cases such as the recent high-profile case of Elizabeth Holmes's trial. We also explore the implications of our framework on the topic of compelled actions that are not necessarily self-incriminatory, and we examine whether our framework offers a useful perspective on the topic of compelled actions that are intended to mislead. We conclude by considering the potential for our framework to be applied to a broader range of topics, and by exploring the potential for our framework to be used as a tool for analysis in other fields. Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. We delve into various methods for understanding neural network fundamentals, visualize the distribution of activations and weights, and examine techniques to enhance overall network performance. This survey serves as a comprehensive guide for researchers seeking to explore the complex world of DNNs and facilitate the development of next-generation networks that combine high computational efficiency with both interpretability and a deeper understanding of their vast capacity. Furthermore, we discuss existing research related to unique neural network architectures that prioritize interpretability over performance. In the realm of computer vision, such architectures include Salford Vector Bessel Filter banks, multi-channel networks, and hyper-layer networks, while in machine learning, examples include local connection networks, tree-structured networks, and soft-k nearest neighbor classifiers. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect to see faster core rotation rates compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that any proposed planetary objects align with our current understanding of the star, and confirmed that KIC 9267654's characteristics fit into established evolutionary tracks. Additionally, we eliminated any alternative explanations for its rotation profile, including magnetic braking effects and core--envelope coupling during the star's main sequence phase. Our research ultimately highlights the importance of monitoring a star's rotation profile throughout its evolution or upon detection, as well as the potential for enhanced angular momentum transport in stars with mass $0.5 M_\sun \leq M_\star \leq 0.8 M_\sun$. Furthermore, we suggest that increased mixing or efficient angular momentum transport could have implications for future stellar models, particularly regarding elements like carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, and ultimately, how these elements are left over or get into planets and other celestial bodies. Lastly, we propose that enhanced angular momentum transport or a planned planetary merger could both be potential explanations for the star's rotation profile, both of which are worthy of exploration in future studies. Therefore, we recommend closely examining other stars with similar rotation profiles, specifically those with relatively slow rotation rates during their main sequence phase, to gain a deeper understanding of this internal rotation pattern, as well as considering the effects of angular momentum transport on future stellar models, and investigating the possibility of planned planetary mergers occurring in giants, which could have implications for future stellar models and the formation and evolution of planets and other celestial bodies. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid construction of false news detection models in response to unexpected events. This proposed framework leverages a small set of labeled data from the target event and utilizes a large amount of unlabeled data from all events to build a diverse pool of base models through contrastive learning. It then employs a meta neural process to build a false news detection model for the target event at the test phase. Extensive experiments have been conducted on the event-driven Wikipedia fake news dataset, and the results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed framework in detecting false news on all events in comparison to the current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the effectiveness of each component of the framework has been verified through a series of controlled experiments. Furthermore, the analysis of the experimental results indicates that the diversity of the base models and the efficiency of the meta neural process have a positive impact on the performance of the proposed framework. Additionally, the flexibility and the generality of the proposed framework have been established through the assessment of its performance in (a) detecting false news on previously unseen domains, (b) detecting false news on previously unseen languages, and (c) detecting false news on previously unseen task types. The proposed framework has achieved superior performance in comparison to the current state-of-the-art methods on all these challenging scenarios. The source code of the proposed framework as well as the experimental results have been made publicly available for the benefit of the research community. The strong suit of the proposed framework lies in its ability to efficiently detect false news on emerging events with limited labeled data, a long-standing challenge in the field of fake news detection. u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals that the valley interference is extremely sensitive to the spatial exchange of electrons between the dopants, and this exchange causes a rotation of the interference pattern by 90 degrees, a phenomenon that cannot be explained by standard theories.
To overcome this limitation, an extended multi-orbital model was devised, accounting for the effects of crystal symmetry, electron spin exchange, and valley interference to describe the phenomenon observed.
The model demonstrates the potential to implement robust and highly versatile quantum simulations using silicon quantum dots. The described mechanism of valley interference also provides insight into designing quantum dots with isolated orbital states, a crucial aspect for quantum computing. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. The algorithm's performance is comparable to a method involving cooperative artificial forces, but our approach provides a more flexible framework for user input and astrobot specifications, making it suitable for real-world applications. The algorithm is designed for high scalability, achieving complete convergence with only a few oscillatory steps on a typical computer. To further improve performance, the algorithm could be optimized for GPU computing. The code is available on GitHub. This research is a part of the SDSS-IV's ongoing development. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring additional modules was introduced, incorporating a new readout system and CMOS analog and digital layers. This study reports on the results of testing the pilot modules from the forward pixel detector, specifically focusing on the reconstruction of hits within the upgraded detector using data collected by the CMS experiment. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources.
An LSTM model was successfully trained to classify the sentiment of Twitter posts,
and its performance was evaluated using the annotated data. Our findings indicate that
the combination of character-level and word-level features can lead to accurate sentiment
classification on Twitter. Furthermore, we discovered that character-level features
play a more significant role than word-level features in this context. Our proposed
character-level feature includes a special sequence that represents the sentiment
of a tweet's hashtags. Our model's performance was the best when using a combination
of character-level and word-level features, and it performed notably well compared
to other popular deep learning classifiers. Our code and trained model are available
on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Additionally, we explored various
hyperparameter settings and established a baseline performance for each model
to facilitate further sentiment analysis research on Twitter. Our study's findings
can be applied to other sentiment-related issues that involve graded classifications.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been developed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we illustrate that entangled states exhibit distinct tomographic features compared to their unentangled counterparts, while states on the edge of synchronization show unique tomographic characteristics that differ from both their fully synchronized and unsynchronized counterparts. These findings provide a foundation for validating the generation of non-classical light states without the need for full state reconstruction. We also discuss potential applications and future research directions in this field. Optical tomograms have the potential to serve as a signature for the specific generation processes producing non-classical light states, offering a chance to explore novel approaches to state reconstruction and to investigate the performance of tomographic reconstruction methods in a realistic scenario. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these objects for computing response functions and the accuracy of our objects being independent of the particular tensor network ansatz used. Additionally, we explore the practical applications of these objects to overcome the limitations of standard tensor network algorithms in terms of quasiperiodic errors and memory requirements. As a result, this study offers a viable solution to the scaling issues that tensor network algorithms face when dealing with systems that are in thermal equilibrium or time-evolved systems. In essence, this research serves as a bridge connecting the traditional tensor network algorithms with more recent approaches that utilize approximate tensor trains through an improvement of the latter's performance by more than an order of magnitude in certain instances. In conclusion, this study affirms the potential effectiveness of tensor network methods in modeling a broad spectrum of situations that are relevant to current and anticipated experimental scenarios. Our findings indicate that there are two critical transition values, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, where $\lambda_1$ represents the minimum rate at which the frog must hop to ensure all points are visited by the walk, and $\lambda_2$ represents the maximum rate at which the walk can cover all points. We demonstrate that $\lambda_1$ is equal to the degree of the infinite tree, $d$, and $\lambda_2$ grows in proportion to $d$ as the number of nodes on the board increases. Additionally, we observe that there are distinct regimes of behavior within the Frog model, specifically delocalization, localization with memory, and periodic behavior, all of which are characterized by the ratio of the frog's hopping rate to the walk's step rate. We also provide a lower bound for the probability of the walk never returning to the origin's starting point. Our analysis relies on a combination of combinatorial techniques, including enumerative counting, and graphical representations, including the use of branching random walks and recursive tree structures. Furthermore, we explore extensions of this behavior to more complex grid structures, including those with multiple layers, as well as scenarios with removal costs for visiting certain points. These extensions reveal that the critical transition values in these cases depend on the degree of the underlying graph structure. Our results also demonstrate connections to existing models, such as the occupancy fraction model, the bootstrap percolation model, and the orientable random walk model, among others. Lastly, we examine open questions and potential future directions for research within the Frog model. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. These labels are then used in a reweighted cross-entropy loss function to train the compact model. The proposed method is tested on various networks and datasets and is shown to be highly effective even in a zero-shot setting. An open-source implementation of the method is also made available. Zero-shot knowledge distillation is particularly relevant to recent advances in deep neural networks due to its practicality and promising results. Two main applications for this method are identified: using a strong network to train multiple compact models, such as in image classification, object detection, and segmentation, and using a collection of strong networks to train a single compact model. The proposed method is evaluated in both a single-source and a multi-source scenario, with positive results. The method faces a trade-off between the level of knowledge transferred and the model's size, with a suggested optimal configuration depending on the scenario. The method's effectiveness is compared to other knowledge distillation methods, with the proposed method showing the best balance between accuracy and model size in a zero-shot setting. The method's source code is also made available for reproducibility purposes. The proposed method faces several challenges, such as how to design efficient decision-based queries and how to incorporate additional information about the input sample, such as its features and semantic meaning. Two potential solutions to these challenges are identified, including incorporating soft labels assigned to the sample's features and its semantic meaning, such as attributes and semantic parts, such as faces, hands, and clothing, which could enhance the proposed reweighted cross-entropy loss function. The method's strength lies in its simplicity, flexibility, and generalizability to a wide range of deep neural network architectures, such as convolutional neural networks, fully connected networks, residual networks, Inception networks, and Transformers. The method's performance is evaluated on a range of computer vision tasks

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. Furthermore, this study explores relationships between strong geodetic subsets and other vertex subsets with distinct properties, such as being a minimum dominating set, an independent set, or a neighborhood cover. These relationships serve as the basis for conjectures on the computational complexity of SG in specific graph types. These conjectures, in turn, have implications on the complexity of other problems, such as Dominating Set and Independent Set. Ultimately, this study aims to establish a deeper understanding of the computational complexity of SG and to explore connections between strong geodetic subsets and other vertex subsets within graphs. Finally, this study proposes future research directions on the computational complexity of SGR and other problems, such as efficient exact algorithms, parameterized complexity, and generalizations of strong geodetic sets. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system's dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a transition model. The learned transition model allows us to incorporate the suboptimal data into a kernelized regularized formulation, resulting in a mixture IQE algorithm with various settings, including using the model to correct policy updates, resulting in a kernelized regularized formulation that can be seen as a mixture of the standard IQE and kernelized regularized episodic reinforcement learning. Our empirical findings indicate significant improvements over baseline imitation learning by incorporating suboptimal data in various tasks, including navigation and robotic grasping, with various amounts of low-quality data. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert knowledge. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce an alternative approach called Co-IL, where imitation learning is combined with fellow agents in a multi-agent setting. By sharing experiences and learning from each other, the cooperative agents can exploit their collective knowledge to speed up learning without needing expert demonstrations. Our proposed Co-IL method explores not only the benefits of inter-agent imitation but also addresses challenges such as credit assignment, where the learning rate is optimized to balance individual learning rates, achieving a balance between exploration and convergence. Our results show that Co-IL outperforms single-agent imitation and traditional reinforcement learning methods by at least 15% in complex tasks on the Fetch and MultiAgent environments. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghr96/Co-Imitation-Learning. With the possibility of cost-free expert demonstrations coming from other agents, our approach could potentially accelerate the training of multiple agents by an order of magnitude. In particular, we observe a significant boost of over 30% in performance when training with only one expert demonstration per agent. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. We also prove and illustrate the trade-off between error-correction performance and decoding computations in PAC codes. Additionally, we provide a computational analysis and a proposed threshold for the number of computations required for sequential decoding. Overall, our findings suggest that low-rate PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance comparable to polar codes with a significantly lower computational complexity. However, high-rate PAC codes exhibit a significant performance degradation due to the polarization effect. As such, they are unlikely to perform well even with very low computational complexity. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our data reveals that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently browse more content from their initial preferred sources. Additionally, we've identified clear partisanship affiliations in users based on the frequency and duration of their browsing habits, ultimately creating a systematic method for assigning partisanship labels in anonymous user data. By analyzing browsing habits over time, we've observed consistent evidence of increasing polarization in online news consumption, with users' browsing habits becoming increasingly segregated along partisan lines. Furthermore, we've investigated the impact of notable news events on users' browsing habits and their effectiveness in reducing online polarization. For instance, we found that users' initial response to the 2020 US presidential election was to increase their online segregation, only to gradually decrease it over time as the news cycle shifted to new topics. At the aggregate level, however, this partial counter to polarization did not offset the broader trend of increasing online segregation. Moreover, we explored the role of online platforms in promoting cross-partisan engagement by analyzing users that consistently browsed content from both liberal and conservative sources, ultimately uncovering the challenges they face in breaking out of their online bubbles. Our research provides a comprehensive exploration of online news consumption habits that can inform the development of platform features to enhance cross-partisan engagement and counter the rise of online polarization. With the increasing dominance of online platforms in shaping our information landscape, understanding the behaviors that contribute to polarization is more crucial than ever. To facilitate replication and further exploration of these trends, we've made our dataset and methodological details openly available. By building on existing research into the Web's influence on polarization, we've gained a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between individual behavior, online environments, and political polarization. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating a multi-task learning approach, the proposed EG-CNNs layer simulates the behavior of an ideal semantic segmentation network. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for parallel, transactional operations across multiple documents. MongoDB's documentation states that transactions can be used across multiple documents, but the accuracy of this claim needs to be verified. To achieve this, we create a formal model representing MongoDB's snapshot isolation and transactional protocols, particularly focusing on snapshot reading and phase-based transactions. We then leverage the model to analyze MongoDB's protocol for updating documents within transactions, revealing that it violates the consistency requirement for snapshot reading. As a result, transactions may leave behind residual documents that are not updated, contradicting MongoDB's documentation. To rectify this issue, we propose an updated protocol for document updates, ensuring that the protocol is consistent and reliable. Unfortunately, this fix compromises the performance of MongoDB's transactions, with an average overhead of up to 106 times the original amount. We also explore alternative solutions to repair the protocol while minimizing performance impact. Finally, we introduce a formal model for validating the updated protocols, ensuring they adhere to the consistency requirements for transactional consistency. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model by applying it to verify the consistency of MongoDB's transactional protocols. Our analysis provides a critical examination of the transactional protocols used in real-world databases like MongoDB, highlighting the importance of rigorous verification to ensure the reliability of such systems. Our work is also relevant to recent research on the leasr amount of isolation needed for real-world databases, demonstrating that in some cases, less isolation can lead to inconsistent results. Our findings are expected to contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussion within the database community regarding the importance of formal verification in database system design. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. The slight discrepancy in the final result could be attributed to the fact that the earlier studies used data from a wider range of approaches, including some that took place during times of increased solar activity. The current observations also provide valuable insights into the overall structure of solar wind energy distributions, with notable features including the average flux levels, the relationship with solar cycle phases, and unusual patterns seen during the approach phases, all of which will continue to be important for the deeper understanding of our sun's coronal plasma, solar wind formation, and the overall structure of our solar system. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  This study is a preliminary exploration and further research is needed to fully comprehend the complex relationship between structure, magnetism, and pressure in BFTO compounds. In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current when comparing single JJs to coupled ones, specifically below T*. Additionally, our findings show that phase log-nary breakdown can occur in SQUIDs when T < T*. Theoretical modeling aligns with our data, providing a better comprehension of the interplay between capacitance, resistance, and temperature on JC dynamics. 

The models illustrate that the switching current's low value and the switching probability distribution's bimodal shape can result from large intrinsic parasitic capacitance, likely including the dielectric's contribution, as well as the effects of quasi-particle interference, although this last factor needs further exploration. Our study offers a deeper understanding of JC dynamics in planar junctions, a crucial step for developing quantum computing with local gate control. 

To bridge the gap between small JC sizes and our measurement techniques, our research incorporates new methods for fabricating and measuring small, epitaxial JJs and SQUIDs. A unique, large-area gate design allows for local temperature control in these tiny devices. Our team also introduces a novel approach for extracting JC characteristics from switching probability measurements.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, the article investigates additional questions related to these problems. It demonstrates that when the underlying space with the property of betweenness is compact, the necessary condition for the existence of an angle function to be equivalent to the necessary condition for it to be continuous. Additionally, the article proves that when the underlying space with the property of betweenness is not compact, there exist spaces with the property of betweenness for which there is an angle function if, and only if there is a continuous angle function. This solution to the second problem is only applicable when the underlying space with the property of betweenness is separable. Furthermore, the article explores distinctness in the context of Euclidean spaces of any finite dimension. It demonstrates that in the context of one-dimensional Euclidean space, a space with the property of betweenness is isomorphic to Euclidean space if, and only if its angle function is order-preserving and induces a linear order on the space. Conversely, it demonstrates that any one-dimensional Euclidean space can be embedded with the property of betweenness for its points, orderable by an angle function. Moreover, it proves that in the context of Euclidean spaces of any dimension greater than one, there is a one-to-one correspondence between such spaces and certain specific types of continua within one-dimensional Euclidean space. Specifically, for any Euclidean space of $n$ dimensions, it can be thought of as the $n$-fold product of one-dimensional Euclidean space with the property of betweeness, and this cross product can be viewed as a certain type of continuum within one-dimensional Euclidean space. Conversely, given any continuum within one-dimensional Euclidean space, it can be mapped bijectively to a space with the property of betweeness for its points, orderable by an angle function, and this space can be embedded in the structure of Euclidean space of $n$ dimensions. We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the strength of fs Raman scattering for pressure detection and ps Raman scattering for pressure and gas composition assessment, our system offers a pressure-sensitive detection approach that is less susceptible to composition fluctuations. As a result, it provides accurate pressure measurements even when oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios are varied. Interestingly, we find that fs Raman scattering can model pressure influences on nitrous Raman shifts more effectively than ps Raman scattering, thus offering two methods for determining gas pressure. Consequently, we demonstrate that fs/ps hybrid rotational CARS can serve as an accurate and reliable probe for analyzing pressure, temperature, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios in gases by combining dual-probe approaches. Notably, pressure estimates derived from both fs and ps Raman scattering shifts show excellent correlation with one another as well as with established calibration curves as we investigate various pressure levels (between 1 bar and 10 bar), temperature (between 293 K and 393 K), and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios (between 0.04 and 0.40). Furthermore, we showcase the capability of this technique to measure these gas properties in a complex, open environment by conducting single-shot measurements in a stationary and moving context. Additionally, we assess the technique's accuracy by comparing measured values to actual standards in both static and dynamic conditions, which reveals a pressure precision of ±0.06 bar, a temperature precision of ±0.75 K, and an N2/O2 precision of ±3.8%. Finally, we explore potential applications of this technique by demonstrating its effectiveness in tracking gas property variations in both steady-flow and stagnation-flow scenarios by leveraging time- and space-resolved measurement capabilities. As such, this dual-probe 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational CARS system offers unparalleled measurement capabilities for temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios in gases across a broad range of applications spanning combustion diagnostics, aerospace research, medical respiratory monitoring, and industrial process control. As a result, this technique provides the most comprehensive and accurate fs/ps hybrid rotational CARS measurements to date, thus opening up a wide range of research opportunities and practical applications in these fields. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. This is particularly beneficial in large-scale decentralized learning applications. The source code for our experiments is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengkehu/DR-DSGD. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Despite the traditional nature of these scams, recent advancements in blockchain technology have created new opportunities for pyramid schemes to operate undetected. This research focuses on the analysis of Forsage, a large-scale pyramid scheme built into a smart contract, and its underlying network of participants. By leveraging data from the blockchain and gathering information from online forums, we assembled a comprehensive dataset comprising thousands of users and detailed information on user rankings within the scheme. Our findings reveal unique aspects of how Forsage's designers incorporated several anti-detection measures into the contract, as well as the explicit inclusion of deceptive artwork, and how these features contributed to the scheme's success. However, the data also exposes the inherent weaknesses of blockchain-based pyramid schemes, revealing how the scheme's rewards structure forces participants to invest more of their own funds in order to stay afloat, the uneven distribution of profits, and the distinct behavioral patterns of participants at different levels of the scheme. Furthermore, our work is an exploration of the integration of pyramid schemes with modern cryptocurrency technology, offering valuable insights that can be applied to the detection of similar schemes built into smart contracts. Ultimately, the data raises critical questions about the role of cryptocurrency exchanges in facilitating these schemes and the effectiveness of current methods for detecting pyramid schemes on the blockchain. For the sake of reproducibility, all collected data and analysis tools are freely available for public use. The data highlights the pressing need for more robust methods of detecting pyramid schemes built into smart contracts and incorporates novel aspects of pyramid scheme behavior that can be applied across historical and modern contexts. The data itself serves as a landmark in the evolution of pyramid schemes and blockchain technology and is essential for any future research in this area. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete despite ongoing efforts to identify new members. The VVV $K$-band survey provides essential data for determining the positions and membership status of globular clusters in the bulge by combining its wide field of view with low extinction in the $K$ band. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory, specifically focusing on models describing semiconductor systems. The conventional method for describing optical responses uses a fine-grid discretization approach, resulting in TB Hamiltonians that are implicitly periodic in photon frequency and spatial coordinates. However, this implicit periodicity may lead to inaccuracies in the modeling of strong light-matter interactions, particularly when involving photon energy exceeding the bandgap or spatially localized light fields. To address this issue, we propose two alternative approaches for capturing optical responses through TB Hamiltonians: first, a compact high-tension representation of the semiconductor's Wigner-Seitz cell; and second, a linearized approximation of photon dispersion relations within the irreducible Brillouin zone. We demonstrate the utility of these methods by comparing predicted absorption spectra with results from full-BZ simulations and by analyzing scattering dynamics of localized light within photonic structures. These techniques enhance the validity of tight-binding models for simulating light-matter interactions, enabling a more accurate simulation of strong interactions and localized light fields. The proposed methods are applicable to various material systems and can be adapted for simulations involving external electric fields and other perturbations. Equilibrium is evaluated by considering networks with a variety of structures, including random, regular, and scale-free networks. The ultimate goal is to assess how these networks respond to an external perturbation. Specifically, we examine how long it takes for the system to return to equilibrium after being disrupted, which represents the network's asymptotic behavior. Our analysis reveals that this response depends heavily on the network's level of interconnectedness. For random and regular networks, the time it takes to reach equilibrium is directly related to the number of unique interactions within the network. In contrast, scale-free networks exhibit a more complex dynamics due to the significant impacts of their highly connected 'hub' nodes. Notably, the time to recovery can be over ten times greater than that of a randomly connected network, providing insight into the delicate balance of networks that we depend on. Additionally, we find that the time to reach equilibrium over all possible states of the network, known as the mixing time, follows a distinct progression for different types of network structures. Our research also uncovers a less expected phenomenon where a higher proportion of attractors exists in a network that has a high number of interconnected components. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Furthermore, our model exhibits comparable performance when compared to state-of-the-art neural GAN-based text generation models while requiring fewer parameters. Our results also highlight the implicit ability of the sparse coding layer to incorporate a form of sentence smoothing, contributing to better performance in low-data setting experiments. Our implementation is available online at https://github.com/ruimengz/sparse_gan. Leveraging sparse codes within the generator section has enabled multiple variants of the SparseGAN framework to be explored, along with their respective advantages anddisadvantages. A comparative analysis of these variants is also provided as part of the supplementary material. In the paper, we explore two primary variants of the sparse coding layer: both a straightforward application and a revised version incorporating a form of temporal soft attention. While both variants prove effective in text generation settings, they still require explicit parameter updates during training, which goes against the original sparse coding concept. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any such algorithm would be capable of achieving a linear approximation ratio in cases where costs are near unit costs. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process involves identifying the conditions under which a specific operator can generate an arbitrary differential equation. On the other hand, the inverse problem seeks to find the simplest form or parametrization of a given differential operator that can generate a specific differential equation. Once the operator is parametrized in its simplest form, determining the compatibility conditions or first integrals of the differential equation becomes straightforward. This paper discusses the minimal parametrization of the Cauchy stress operator for a one-dimensional heat conduction equation with thermal conductivity $k(x,t)$ and focuses on relaxing the requirement that $k(x,t)$ be positive-definite. It is demonstrated that removing this limitation enables the consideration of a broader class of non-skew symmetric operators, leading to novel first integrals or compatibility conditions of the heat conduction equation. The proposed generalization of the Cauchy operator is applicable to partial differential equations and is thus of broad interest. Furthermore, this study establishes that the relaxation of the positive-definite requirement for $k(x,t)$ facilitates the construction of closed loops, thereby providing a solution for the inverse problem of partial differential equations. This advancement is theoretically relevant to nonlinear partial differential equations, although the demonstration of this fact is theoretically concept-based rather than proof-based. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By incorporating dissipation, we find that only even photon bundles survive, while odd bundles are scattered, and we observe the emergence of a critical slowness in qubit flip gate operations due to this protection. This paritiesymmetry-protected bundle emission provides a potential means for detecting and controlling qubit flip gate operations. Furthermore, it gives rise to the generation of odd photons through the scattering of even photons, offering a novel paritiesymmetry-protected two-photon transition process. Experimental verification of this theory is also outlined. The model also extends to other types of symmetries, such as phase and time-reversal symmetry, resulting in the production of photon bundles with specific polarization or temporal characteristics. This paritiesymmetry-protected bundle emission process is unique to the ultrastrong coupling regime and may also occur in other systems exhibiting similar dynamics. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The new approach shows comparable convergence rates and constraints satisfaction levels as standard conformal finite element methods. The development of this method enables a broader exploration of initial data configurations that can be used in simulations of numerical relativity. The approach is applicable to multiple 3D numerical relativity codes and the underlying theory is explained in a way that is accessible to researchers in the numerical relativity community. Furthermore, we outline an extension of this method that can be used in combination with effective action formulations. The novel approach is relevant to current and planned multi-GPU numerical relativity simulations, as well as future simulations involving rotating stars and binary neutron star mergers with fundamental field physics. The implementation of this method in the [TTUK] numerical relativity code has been made publicly available for download. The code is an extension of the initial data solver within the [TTUK] code and incorporates multiple GPU acceleration using the PyCUDA library. The code has been used to generate a range of initial data configurations that can be used in numerical relativity simulations and the results have been compared to standard conformal finite element methods. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking tasks, delivering outstanding results. Nonetheless, numerous challenges hinder their widespread adoption due to costly and time-consuming data labeling processes. Knowledge distillation can effectively compress multiple models trained on labeled data by sharing an ensemble of logits from each model, thereby producing a viable and more compact ranking model. Nonetheless, several limitations in existing knowledge distillation methods hinder their full potential, including: (1) only utilizing a single model's output; (2) relying solely on labeled data for iteration; and (3) failing to account for the discrepancies between models. To address these constraints and enhance the performance of the base model, we introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel knowledge distillation framework that addresses the aforementioned challenges. PILE combines the outputs from multiple models, leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data through iterative refinement and matching, as well as structural optimization to minimize the discrepancies between models, thereby producing a precise and reliable ranking model. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate substantial gains in ranking performance, with improvements reaching up to +0.19 in NDCG, compared to standalone models and strong baselines, cementing PILE's efficacy and potential for broad application in ranking tasks. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly increased data quantity, posing new challenges for traditional analysis methods. To address these challenges, researchers are turning to multiple facets of machine learning for enhanced data interpretation, accelerated analysis, and optimized experimental design. By integrating machine learning into user facilities, the speed and efficiency of research can be substantially improved, allowing for more rapid discovery of top-notch materials. This paper explores the potential of machine learning to streamline experiments at synchrotron radiation facilities and to hasten the analysis of large datasets, thereby accelerating material development and exploration. Through examples from experiments conducted at the National Synchrotron Light Source II, we demonstrate how machine learning can be used to optimize experimental design, refine crystal structure, and efficiently classify materials, thus unlocking vast possibilities for the development of novel materials with desired functions. Furthermore, we highlight opportunities for machine learning to enhance accessibility, scalability, and efficiency in research, and outline future directions for the integration of machine learning into user facilities. By embracing machine learning, researchers can accelerate material discovery, optimization, and development, making it a valuable tool for the development of advanced functional materials. Additionally, we highlight how machine learning can promote inclusivity and address the current shortage of experts in analytical techniques by enabling remote high-throughput operations and facilitating real-time feedback and guidance. As such, machine learning has the potential to revolutionize research at user facilities and beyond. Furthermore, we outline several challenges and opportunities for machine learning integration into user facilities, highlighting potential paths for future research and development, and emphasizing the need for a broader discussion on the integration of machine learning into such facilities. This discussion should focus on the potential benefits, challenges, and future directions, as well as the development of guidelines and best practices for the integration of machine learning into research at user facilities. This, in turn, will enable a more seamless collaboration between experimental and machine learning researchers, and will facilitate the integration of machine learning into such facilities, promoting a more efficient and effective development of advanced functional materials. As such, this discussion should be a starting point for a broader exchange of ideas within the research community. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence term may actually facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, with the side effect of reviving quantum fluctuations despite the destructive effects of decoherence. Furthermore, we observe that this phenomenon can also occur when non-stoquastic terms are introduced only during the annealing process rather than being present throughout, with implications for the potential development of quantum algorithms resistant to decoherence and even the enhancement of quantum annealing's performance in real-world applications. Furthermore, we propose that block-sparse Hamiltonians may serve as another means of achieving successful ground states through QA. Lastly, we discuss the possibility of constructing block-sparse Hamiltonians that retain non-stoquastic characteristics yet remain manageable for quantum annealing. Ultimately, we conclude that the principles underlying successful ground-state achievement through quantum annealing may prove invaluable for the development of new quantum algorithms. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning technique utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed technique also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghr96/local-critic-training and has been successfully applied to various benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Movie Rating Prediction. The proposed method achieves a notable improvement over parallel learning techniques currently in use, with an average enhancement of 18% when compared to the best alternative. The technique also outperforms batch norm by achieving a 12% improvement in accuracy. The paper also explores the integration of local critic training with existing optimization techniques, including batch norm, by demonstrating that it surpasses its effectiveness by 2%. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes.
However, the dispersed nature of nanofillers within the matrix creates a complex conductivity pattern, making it challenging to accurately pinpoint the extent of damage.
Existing methods primarily offer vague estimations of maximum damage extent, without considering the intricate geometry of the matrix.
To address this issue, a precise algorithm is proposed to determine the exact shape of damage by initially utilizing a simulated model of the material's conductivity, then applying a genetic algorithm to minimize the difference between the simulated and actual electrical field distributions.
The proposed method is tested on simulated data corresponding to various quadrilateral damage shapes, demonstrating an accuracy of $10^{-3}$ in terms of area and $10^{-2}$ in terms of perimeter when comparing the detected to actual shapes.
The algorithm's efficiency is further validated by applying it to experimental data collected from a 2D scanning process, successfully identifying a rectangular damage shape with a genetic algorithm optimization. The developed method provides a framework for refining the detection results using multiple scans by integrating the output of each scan as an initial population, resulting in an enhanced estimation of a triangular damage shape with a precision of around $10^{-2}$ in both area and perimeter. The proposed approach is suitable for monitoring large-scale engineering projects by enabling the detection of relatively small damages within relatively large, self-sensing composite panels. The genetic algorithm-based technique is computationally demanding but shows great potential for optimizing the material's properties on a microscopic level, and could potentially be integrated with other imaging methods for enhanced performance. We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in situations where there is only limited information about the dynamics, the environment, or both. It stands out especially in environments that have never been experienced before, or in scenarios where previous knowledge can be leveraged to some extent. By drawing on past experiences, the algorithm can adapt to new situations more efficiently. It breaks down complex tasks into a series of continuous control problems with varying penalties, using the available information to make decisions. Through simulation, we showed that it can learn to control a range of systems with different dynamics on our testbed, an underactuated aerial robot. This includes learning to balance, move forward, and fly in a single trial, using only a small amount of high-fidelity data and relying on low-cost sensor readings for guidance. Interestingly, we found that by altering the penalties, the algorithm can explore different trajectories, and in some cases, it discovered an equilibrium where it alternates between two different behavior patterns. We also observed that it can sometimes get stuck in a state where the learned action has a significant impact, but the algorithm is unable to change this. We addressed this by adding a new term to the cost function, but further research is needed to fully understand these states. Overall, our method holds promise for using a wide range of data to control complex systems, and could potentially be more efficient than other methods in certain situations. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of advanced prosthetic devices for walking. The study demonstrates the feasibility of recovering a range of gait information from ECoG signals with high accuracy, offering a promising avenue for the development of reliable and precise BCIs for lower limb rehabilitation. The high accuracy achieved in this study surpasses previous EEG-based studies, suggesting that the higher spatial and temporal resolution of ECoG recordings, coupled with the closer electrode placement to the brain, yield significantly more precise predictions of complex walking dynamics. The research has implications for the creation of advanced prosthetic devices capable of responding to a wide range of commands, stepping speeds, and other critical aspects, ultimately enhancing their usability and effectiveness. The study's findings provide a solid foundation for exploring how this BCI can be applied to different walking environments and potentially adapted for use in intracortical implants, such as the Neurochip, which feature a larger number of closely spaced electrodes that provide even higher resolution recordings. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. These examples demonstrate how NS-ES outperforms conventional methods and overcomes difficulties in quantifying entropy and information when working with limited or noisy data. The accompanying code allows users to apply these ideas to their own NS implementations. Furthermore, this work paves the way for exploring other application areas of Nested Sampling, such as assessing model performance and bias. The proposed technique can also be adapted for weighted sampling schemes, further enhancing its versatility. Ultimately, this paper shows that by combining Nested Sampling and NS-ES, it becomes possible to efficiently estimate a broader range of quantities, like maximum likelihood estimators, correlations, and standard deviations, even when dealing with intricate distributions and limited data sets. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed probability matrix that encapsulates the temporal evolution of directed connections between brain regions. DECENNT leverages this representation to forecast new temporal connectivity patterns based on past relationships. By integrating region-specific feature extraction and temporal prediction, DECENNT outperforms existing methods on multiple task benchmarks, providing a comprehensive solution for dynamic graph prediction. Moreover, our analysis showcases the efficacy of DECENNT in identifying functional brain regions responsible for initiating and sustaining connectivity patterns. Overall, DECENNT sets a new standard for dynamic graph prediction, extending beyond classification capabilities to a more fundamental understanding of connectivity phenomena.
