Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can then be compared to observed data to estimate evolutionary parameters. Despite the abundance of phylogenetic network generators, a lack of comparison among these models hinders our understanding of their topological characteristics and resulting outcomes. This study compares the topological features of six phylogenetic network generators, including binary and reticulate trees, assessing their conformity to standard power laws and the distributional similarities of resulting trees or networks. Our analysis reveals that some generators conform to power laws and distributional standards, whereas others deviate from these expectations, implying that certain models may provide more accurate representations of evolutionary processes. By evaluating and differentiating the topological properties of these generators, this study provides a wealth of reference data for researchers to guide their choice of phylogenetic network generator for specific applications and data sets. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of thorough validation and characterization of phylogenetic network generators through comparative analysis of their output, ensuring that these tools accurately capture the intricate details of evolutionary processes. This validation process can be applied to other phylogenetic network generators, reticulate tree construction methods, and statistical phylogenetic analysis tools. The study's findings and data are available through an interactive online interface, enabling effortless exploration and comparison of the generators' performance. In conclusion, this research emphasizes the necessity for transparent and accessible validation of phylogenetic analysis tools to ensure their reliable use in informing scientific interpretations and driving further discovery. This is particularly crucial in the field of phylogenetics, where the accuracy of results directly depends on the performance of these tools. As such, this study is a significant step towards elevating the standards of phylogenetic research and fostering collaboration among researchers and practitioners in the field. Ultimately, this will ultimately contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex evolutionary processes that have shaped the diversity of life on Earth. To this end, this study is freely available to the research community, and the data presented within its findings is openly accessible to facilitate replication and further exploration. As such, this study is a landmark achievement in the field of phylogenetics, and a model for transparent and collaborative research that will undoubtedly inspire a new generation of scientists

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features in video footage is presented for this purpose. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are offered to support the proposed detection method. A newly designed network that combines convolutional neural network and recurrent neural network structures achieves the best detection results to date. A proposed framework that combines detection and biolocomotion classification results in a high accuracy rate of 92% in recognizing biological movement, alongside a 6-fold reduction in detection latency. A mobile app built using the developed detection approach successfully engaged participants in identifying biological movement in a real-world setting. A preliminary analysis of the app's data reveals that users' primary biolocomotion-related activities in a national park are animal watching and photography. A more efficient version of the detection algorithm, achieved through a method called progressive fine-tuning, yields a significant 2-fold decrease in training latency without compromising biolocomotion detection performance. The trained model's performance remains steady at around 85% across different dataset batch sizes. Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to generalize is demonstrated across various video resolution levels. A new, more comprehensive biolocomotion dataset created in a controlled laboratory environment, along with the existing datasets, sets a new standard for biolocomotion research. An analysis of data distribution reveals that current deep learning approaches tend to overfit rare moving biological entities. A novel, simplified biolocomotion detection algorithm based on a single feature, along with improvements to the progressive fine-tuning method, results in a substantial 3-fold increase in training latency reduction.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The algorithm is particularly well-suited for GPU acceleration, allowing for the efficient handling of massive matrices with minimal memory access, and has been implemented in C++/CUDA and is available for download. Extensive numerical experiments have validated the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrated excellent performance on various real-world applications, including graph Laplacian eigenvalue problems, matrix factorization, and data reweighting, with up to 16 times speedup over state-of-the-art methods on large-scale matrices. The Nested Neumann method has the lowest memory usage among all comparable methods examined, with memory access patterns that are friendly to GPU architecture. The method has been found to be highly robust to parameter settings, with little impact on accuracy in the presence of over-tuning. The method has also been found to be suitable for distributed computing on multiple GPUs with minimal modifications, and has been successfully applied to large-scale machine learning applications, including semi-supervised learning, multi-task learning, and support vector machines. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Furthermore, we propose an experimental verification of topological Anderson phases using a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model constructed from an optical waveguide and coupled atomic resonators. Our theoretical model is subsequently applied to simulate the topological Anderson phases, showing good agreement with our theoretical predictions. Finally, we investigate the effect of binary disorders on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model using numerical simulations, verifying that they accurately reproduce our findings. In conclusion, our research provides valuable insights into the topological and localization phenomena induced by random binary disorders in one-dimensional systems. Furthermore, we outline the technical specifications for building an experimental setup capable of producing topological Anderson phases. In particular, we detail the specifications for an optical waveguide and coupled atomic resonators, highlighting the importance of controlling the interaction between the waveguide and the atomic system to produce the desired topological phases. Last, we consider potential extensions to higher-dimensional systems and the role of correlated disorders in topological quantum electronics. This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. While such relationship can be demonstrated for certain parameter choices, others reveal a more intricate geometric framework involving multiple curves to fully capture the relationship in question. The study provides a framework for further exploring genus one geometry through the lens of geometric mathematics. The investigation into the curves' properties, including their degrees, birational connections, and geometric dimensions, can be seen as an extension of the approach introduced in the companion paper. The study concludes with an examination of the curves' connection to elliptic double-box integrals in $d=2$ and $d=4$ dimensions. While the former is characterized by a rational part and massless propagators, the latter requires a pass in the Feynman parameter approach, resulting in an expression over $\mathbb{Z}$ but without explicit connection to the elliptic curve. The study provides a closing reflection on the potential connections between genus one geometry and other geometric structures within sunset and double-box integrals. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under suitable conditions. All results have a broader implications for linearity testing in dynamic models. A simulation study and empirical analysis are also conducted to evaluate the tests' performance. The results show the tests' accuracy in evaluating linearity and model fit. The developed linearity tests can be applied to dynamic models through the R package netGJ, with linearity testing functions available within. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. The work also underscores the significance of explicit expressions for derivatives in the forward pass, allowing the utilization of explicit and implicit methods for numerical solution mapping resolution. The proposed techniques are subsequently incorporated into declarative network frameworks, demonstrating the efficacy of explicit and semi-implicit resolutions for the optimal transport and vector pooling problems, respectively. The developed models are evaluated on diverse datasets, yielding superior performance in our experiments. The study offers a comprehensive exploration of declarative network design, emphasizing the critical role of forward pass computations in both performance and scalability. The work is subsequently repurified to offer a unified framework for developing efficient implicit algorithms in optimization domains. The research is further extended to provide a declarative network framework that can handle nonsmooth objective functions by integrating a generalised semi-implicit resolution mapping. The study is subsequently applied to provide a optimal transport framework that can handle signed entities by developing a novel extension to the 2OT problem. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed framework integrates multiple scales, incorporates rate-dependent and independent reactions, accounts for living components that respond to stimuli in a non-deterministic manner, and includes advection terms to model protein transfer on lipid membranes. This work provides a comprehensive overview of the variables, laws, and boundary conditions involved in the proposed framework. Furthermore, we derive simplified equations for specific cellular phenomena, such as spreading, locomotion, and the redistribution of proteins across lipid membranes, demonstrating that the proposed framework is a versatile and adaptable framework for the study of cell dynamics. This approach can also be applied to investigate other living systems that involve the movement of proteins across membranes and the reorganization of actin networks within cells. This work is presented in a way that is accessible to a broad audience and is premised on the idea that complex biological systems can be studied using interdisciplinary approaches that combine engineering, biology, and mathematics. This work is an extension of previous research presented at the 2019 and 2020 Biomechanics and Motion Analysis Symposium. Additionally, we provide a written account of our previously presented research in this manuscript. This work is an outcome of the collaboration between biologists and biomechanical engineers who shared their expertise and laboratory observations to further our understanding of cell dynamics. This collaborative approach involved the exchange of knowledge and laboratory data, with biomechanical engineers providing mathematical models that were informed by the biological community's expertise and laboratory observations. This process of knowledge sharing and the refinement of mathematical models using biological knowledge led to a deeper understanding of the complex phenomena underlying cell dynamics. This understanding was further solidified through the discussion of model predictions with the biological community, ensuring that the models accurately reflected the underlying mechanisms that govern cell behavior. This collaborative approach to research is an exemplary model for the way that knowledge should be generated in the scientific community, with a clear emphasis on the importance of interplay between theoretical and experimental approaches in the study of complex biological systems. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. The implementation of our methods on the Ethereum blockchain resulted in a significant reduction in false positives, yielding a 98% true positive rate. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we demonstrate the general surface code decay performance threshold to be 0.96, indicating that decent performance can be achieved with only limited experience in environments where errors frequently occur. Our research also reveals the value of learning from diverse noise scenarios and the importance of considering faulty measurements, with further improvements seen in scenarios where errors are uncommon. Our optimized codes provide improved performance metrics and demonstrate the surface code decay threshold to be a maximum entropy threshold. Finally, we outline a plan for extending this noise-resistant learning approach to other quantum error correction codes. The associated code for this study has been made publicly available on the Quantum Machine Learning GitHub repository. Furthermore, we have introduced a new challenge for the Quantum Machine Learning GitHub repository, centered on the development of topological quantum error correction codes using Quantum-Assisted Learning. Cloud-based HPC deployments can provide cost savings and optimal resource allocation.
However, there are significant differences between the network architectures of cloud and on-premise HPC systems.
These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.
Initially, the investigation focuses on latency, bandwidth, and data transfer patterns in small-scale tests, followed by simulations on a larger scale.
Validation is conducted across multiple cloud providers and HPC systems, revealing that system noise and variability can substantially impact both performance and cost at both small and large scales. 
In particular, the findings indicate that existing fault tolerance mechanisms may actually decrease scalability in certain situations.
Furthermore, the results show that user-provided noise can influence the behavior of commercial HPC clusters, potentially leading to suboptimal resource allocation.
In contrast, a system that takes network noise into account, particularly variability in latency and data transfer, can result in better performance, reduced costs, and enhanced scalability.
Finally, the research highlights the importance of noise modeling in the development of efficient, scalable, and cost-effective cloud HPC applications. 
In conclusion, while cloud HPC deployments present several challenges, they also offer numerous opportunities for innovation in the field. 
As such, the development of specialized network protocols, noise modeling, and more effective fault tolerance and resource allocation strategies is crucial for fully realizing the potential of cloud-based HPC. 
The research presented in this study can serve as a foundation for the exploration of these opportunities and the development of more effective cloud HPC applications. 
The corresponding code and data are available online at the specified URLs. 
Future research directions on cloud HPC noise modeling, resource allocation, and application development are also discussed in this paper. 
In particular, the study proposes the creation of an open-source, cloud-agnostic HPC benchmark suite that incorporates real-world network noise and variability for the purpose of evaluating and comparing the performance, scalability, and cost efficiency of different cloud HPC providers and systems. 
This benchmark suite has the potential to contribute meaningfully to the advancement of cloud-based high-performance computing. 
As such, we invite researchers and industry professionals to collaborate with us on this endeavor. 
The proposed benchmark suite can offer numerous benefits to both academia and the private sector, including the opportunity to investigate various research directions, evaluate and compare different cloud HPC systems, and develop more effective, scalable, and cost-efficient cloud HPC applications.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model being highly applicable to various real-world challenges like personalized advertising and medicine selection. It involves a learner making decisions for a learning agent that interacts with an environment. Unlike traditional multi-armed bandit learning, contextual linear bandits incorporates rich context information to inform these decisions. We have developed a groundbreaking new approach, called DISCO, that allows multiple learners to collaborate, sharing only their final actions and obtained rewards, enabling the overall best policy to be learned through standard contextual linear bandits methods. DISCO is highly efficient as it is no-regret in both non-contextual and contextual linear bandits, guaranteeing the fastest possible learning. Moreover, DISCO requires the fewest possible communication exchanges between learners, minimizing communication costs. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of DISCO, showcasing its significant advantages over existing methods, particularly in scenarios with limited data and strong context. As the first solution, DISCO extends significantly previous positive results on its own merit. Moreover, combining DISCO with standard contextual linear bandits algorithms yields near-optimal regret bounds, providing the first concrete answers to fundamental questions. Finally, we have also investigated a natural extension of DISCO, revealing that a significant performance gain comes from reducing the context sharing. All DISCO algorithms, along with their theoretical analysis, are rigorously proved within the standard multi-armed bandits and contextual linear bandits frameworks. Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Ultimately, findings from these experiments support the idea that initial geometric conditions lead to a highly correlated and elliptic flow-dependent radial expansion of the medium.  However, results disagree with predictions made by hydrodynamic models that claim a flow-independent radial expansion.  Additionally, data show that events with higher-than-average elliptic flow exhibit greater elliptic flow anisotropy than expected from the average geometric condition, indicating initial conditions exhibit greater than average elliptic anisotropy.  Two different event shape cuts were analyzed to gain further understanding of initial conditions and the resulting flow. Lastly, findings from these experiments support the idea that initial geometric conditions play a key role in the subsequent development of the medium in these collisions. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and combined it with existing models for flow simulations, resulting in accurate simulation outcomes for particle size and distribution in both steady and turbulent flows. Our algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to standard methods for reducing computational costs while maintaining precision. Furthermore, we examine the influence of collision time steps, flow time steps, and particle size on our algorithm's behavior. Our proposed method showcases notable gains in simulation efficiency without compromising accuracy, making it an optimal choice for simulating complex multiphase flows with numerous particles on high-performance computing platforms. Our algorithm also facilitates realistic simulation outcomes for particles experiencing varying flow conditions, including those experiencing extended periods without collisions, interactions with other particles, or both. Finally, we provide practical guidelines for selecting optimal collision and flow time steps for different particle sizes and flow scenarios. Our research focuses on two highly regarded simulation models, incorporating similar improvements which could be adapted to other simulation techniques. Overall, our integrated algorithm offers a reliable solution for accurately simulating multiphase flows at the single-particle and multi-particle levels. As computational power continues to advance towards realistic collision time steps without artificial lengthening, our algorithm will provide a precise simulation method for particle behavior in flows. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors by 70%. Furthermore, control system performance was examined under various terrain parameters, revealing how changes in friction and stiffness affect robot behavior. These findings have implications for the design of higher-order legged robots. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators assess the reasoning skills of these models by means of a series of complex, multi-choice questions. CONDAQA differentiates itself from existing datasets through its exclusive focus on negation. We anticipate that benchmarking models on this novel dataset will provide valuable insights into the capabilities of current natural language processing systems and offer a challenging test of their generalization abilities beyond domain-specific evaluations. CONDAQA is presently the only comprehensive reading comprehension dataset incorporating a variety of negation cues, making it an important milestone in the development of natural language understanding technologies capable of accurately processing negation in all contexts. CONDAQA is available for public access through this repository: https://github.com/AsifKhanNiazi/CONDAQA. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. The performance of HDTM is on par with specialized, non-distributed techniques like LDA-Hier, but it surpasses their scalability by several orders of magnitude. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined by quenching's initial conditions, and that distinct quenching trajectories correspond to unique ground states, implying that the annealing gap's variability is a manifestation of the system's large degeneracy within the parameter-space. Furthermore, our findings indicate that quenching can surpass the limitations imposed by quantum annealing when combined with efficient dipole-driven quantum dynamics. As a result, both quantum annealing and quenching hold promise as solution paths for tackling complex, intricate systems, with each approach offering a unique path to overcoming the annealing gap. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the interplay between quantum annealing and quenching can yield unprecedented gains in system performance. As such, we propose the concept of "quantum quenching trajectories," which can be designed with various techniques, such as machine learning, to create optimized trajectories that efficiently bypass the annealing gap, leading to a breakthrough where the system's performance surpassing that of quantum annealing and quenching dynamics. Additionally, we explore the application of our findings to the exact cover problem, a computationally demanding NP-complete problem, and present a novel quantum algorithm that leverages both quantum annealing and quenching to achieve an optimal solution with a reduced number of qubits. This model is a good representation of infinite-layer nickelate materials when it exhibits an electron-filled band that is separated from the d-x*y band due to screening, thus preventing charge transfer and lattice distortion around the nickel sites. However, in the case of lanthanum nickelate, this isolated band gets filled with electrons as we decrease the Coulomb repulsion between electrons on the d-yz band. For both materials, we find that a type of pairing that causes opposition to superconductivity can be weakened by lattice vibrations and becomes irrelevant at low temperatures, allowing for the possibility of superconductivity to arise. We also examine whether a type of pairing that relies on the separation of the d-x*y and d-yz bands can occur in lanthanum nickelate when the bands are not fully separated due to screening. Although this kind of pairing is highly sensitive to the distance of separation between the bands, it can be weakened by lattice vibrations and electron orbital distortions, leading to the possibility of competing with the electron-filled band and affecting the superconducting state. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive investigation of pairing interactions in infinite-layer nickelate materials that involve electron orbital distortions and lattice coupling. This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space, specifically focusing on initial conditions with non-negative values. By leveraging a variation of the cutoff Boltzmann equation and expanding on earlier work, it has been demonstrated that even minimal collisions can generate significant mixing effects, leading to the convergence of solutions towards a global minimum or maximum according to their sign. Additionally, the existence of a global maximum or minimum under collisional forces that are polynomially related to the particle velocity has been established, providing insight into the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation. Furthermore, by applying a similar approach, it has been shown that even discrete weak collisions can result in a similar mixing phenomenon, known as Taylor dispersion. This phenomenon, identified in partial differential equations, arises from the interaction of collisional forces and transport processes, causing distinct modes of the solution to spread at varying speeds. As a result, different frequency components of the solution will eventually exhibit overlapping regions of influence, resulting in an optimal spacing that determines the rate of this dispersion. This optimal spacing can be found by minimizing a specific expression under certain constraints, providing a clear answer to a previously open question regarding the scaling of this optimal spacing. Finally, by expanding on earlier work involving the cutoff Boltzmann equation, a more detailed analysis is conducted on the scaling of this optimal spacing, as well as its relation to other quantities, such as the maximal impact time and the optimal spacing in one-dimensional cases. Additionally, a more general strategy is introduced for addressing similar problems involving other transport equations, such as the Vlasov equation, by employing a modification of these equations that captures the essential features of these phenomena. As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. This is accompanied by a $2$-approximation algorithm for the general anti Tai mapping problem on unordered trees, achievable within $O(|V_1|^3|V_2|^3)$ time. We analyze and compare our results with existing approaches, particularly highlighting the improvements made by our anti Tai mapping-related proposals. These proposals are implemented and tested on various realistic datasets, showcasing their effectiveness. The anti Tai mapping framework is also shown to provide a suitable relaxation for the Tai mapping problem within different applications, outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods, as evidenced by the achieved results. The source code for our experiments is provided alongside the supplementary material, along with a detailed explanation of the algorithmic implementations and the experimental design. We explore potential future extensions for the anti Tai mapping objective function, introducing new problems such as the bi-Tai mapping problem, and present a generic approximation algorithm for problems defined as constrained maximum-weight matchings in directed acyclic graphs. We conclude by outlining the broader implications of the anti Tai mapping framework within graph theory and signal processing. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems and may be triggered by the interaction between gas streams moving at different speeds, especially in their outer regions. This paper explores the effects of dust settling on VSI by running multiple numerical simulations of partially settled particle systems. It was discovered that VSI can occur beyond 10 astronomical units (AU) in disks with low solar mass stars even without considering dust growth. However, the presence of instabilities is hindered in regions beyond 20-30 AU due to the excessive vertical extension of gas streams. Combining the simulations with models of particle growth revealed that VSI can extend as far as 50-60 AU in areas with low shear rates. The presence of instabilities in such regions accelerates the growth of particles, making them available for further growth into solid bodies. It was also found that VSI can cause the mixing of particles even as far as 100 AU in regions with low shear rates. This implies that particles can grow into bodies like asteroids and comets in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Additionally, our research includes a corollary related to the study of complex projective spaces with certain properties. Specifically, within these spaces, we can demonstrate that certain types of polynomial growth harmonic functions are actually constant, provided that they are defined within the context of a particular mapping. This insight provides valuable evidence in supporting a long-standing conjecture regarding the curvature of these spaces. Furthermore, our findings also provide a solution to an alternative form of this conjecture. The techniques employed in this research involve a combination of Hamilton's focus shift technique and a method for analyzing the curvature of these spaces, in addition to a number of other harmonic map-related results. These techniques, coupled with a detailed examination of the algebraic structure of these spaces, collectively enable the proof of this key theorem and its associated corollary. Notably, one of the harmonic map-related results that is utilized in the proof has an independent interest of its own. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Additionally, SIMC 2.0 introduces an alternative secure computation approach for non-linear layers, such as ReLU and softmax, by distributing the computation across both client and server sides. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate the enhanced performance of SIMC 2.0, resulting in up to 6.6 times faster linear layer computations, 1.5 times faster non-linear layer computations, and the successful execution of complex ML models, including image classification and clustering. As a result, SIMC 2.0 surpasses previous benchmarks in both throughput and latency, meeting the high-performance standards required for critical applications. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 ensures the security of various ML tasks by providing a secure barometer and demonstrating the effective concealment of sensitive information. With improvements in both efficiency and security, SIMC 2.0 sets a new standard for secure ML computations. Moreover, the source code of SIMC 2.0 has been openly disseminated, paving the way for the exploration of additional secure computation protocols. Ultimately, this research underscores the feasibility of securing real-world ML applications through the implementation of efficient and secure protocols. Although certain configurations of SIMC 2.0 may compromise some degree of model accuracy, the scope of this research focuses on the enhancement of secure ML computations rather than model training. As such, the associated code is built on top of established open-source repositories, with specific modifications tailored to meet the requirements of secure computation. Consequently, this research does not address fundamental challenges in model training but rather addresses the issue of protecting real-world ML models from an untrusted client. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, the long-term financial implications are more complex to assess due to various factors including future earnings on violence-reducing offenses, potential future incarceration, and future healthcare needs. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This model also reveals that the clusters within the raft behave similarly to those found in sub-critical regimes of pinning barriers. A notable feature of this model is that it predicts a highly disorderly state of fragments once the particles reassemble faster than the rate at which the surrounding fluid is expanding. This is because shorter clusters then become unstable and break into two smaller ones, a trend that has been confirmed by our experiments as well as previous observations made under other stretching conditions. This finding of ours also extends its influence to other situations where a layer of floating particles is broken up over time, such as when it is displaced from its equilibrium by a passing object. The model we've developed can also be applied to more complex situations, like the spreading of a fluid over a layer of floating particles, which creates a mixture that can either break up over time or remain stable for long periods, depending on factors like how quickly the particles reassemble and the ratio of the depth of the fluid to the size of the clusters within the raft. This knowledge of ours can be further expanded to encompass layers of particles floating over non-Newtonian fluids by modifying the rules of our model to account for the unique properties of these fluids. A major consequence of how a raft made of particles breaks up when expanded is that it cannot be put back together in a seamless manner once it has reached a certain level of fragmentation, a phenomenon that could have implications for how biological membranes work. A notable feature of this model of ours is that it can also be applied to understand the behavior of layers of living cells that are being stretched apart, a situation that is akin to how membranes are broken up when a cell is pulled apart by a force like a tight grip. We focus on networks that utilize $k$-way comparators, where the number of inputs $k$ is specified. Our primary goal is to create a sorting network with a limited number of layers, using comparators with $k$ inputs. In particular, we aim to establish a minimum number of layers required to sort $n$ objects for any $n$ that can be divided by $k$. We investigate this question for values of $k$ that are both small and quite large. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. We further outline an appropriate test for new two-fluid solutions by linking them to their respective single-fluid components and thus to established stars, whereas previously unknown solutions would indicate new, ground-state anisotropic stars. Two new family names, 'Wang-Zhang' and 'Liu-Lan', are proposed to describe these two-fluid solution sets. Six specific solution prototypes are then defined across both families to demonstrate our theoretical framework. Furthermore, we investigate regularity at the star's center for both fluids, establishing conditions on their central energy densities and pressures. Lastly, we outline a method for evaluating any proposed two-fluid star's energy density profile. This approach is universally applicable to both the Wang-Zhang and Liu-Lan families. We then proceed to examine the Liu-Lan type-I solutions' behavior in relation to mass-eigenvalue relationships, confirming that prototypes fitting the testing criteria yield viable, anisotropic relativistic star solutions. This study provides a framework for investigating two-fluid stars within General Relativity.

In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness criterion. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness criterion must be satisfied in an extensive manner. Finally, we established that for any mechanism with more than two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations must not always induce fair allocations up to one good. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets. Our code is now openly accessible for exploration. In addition, we outline a new evaluation metric, termed 'category coverage', to provide a more comprehensive assessment of UDA performance. According to this measure, our approach outperforms previous work by a substantial 5.3% on the GTA-to-Cityscapes adaptation task. Furthermore, we demonstrate that simply employing a stochastic version of our previous protocol, which incorporates source domain supervision, yields a notable 3.6% improvement over the current record on this same task. In essence, our research highlights the value of exploring alternative domain representation models in UDA. Moreover, we highlight the importance of incorporating category information into both source and target mappings to enhance the effectiveness of adaptations. Lastly, we highlight the scope for the development of novel neural mapping techniques in UDA that surpass current state-of-the-art protocols. Additionally, our data is consistent with the quark mass being evenly distributed between the quark and the antiquark as expected in the massless quark limit. Lastly, our results can potentially inform the interpretation of lattice data in the context of chiral effective field theory. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. However, existing approaches to computing the Shapley value for training examples in the context of the FairML algorithm have several limitations, including the use of approximated values, reliance on a predetermined model subset, and a training process that starts from scratch for each subset. This paper introduces an efficient and precise method for computing the exact Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness in the presence of noise, and showcases its effectiveness on large-scale machine learning datasets. The proposed approach is complementary to existing machine learning tools and is highly adaptable, allowing it to be seamlessly integrated into various machine learning pipelines. The technique is particularly well-suited for debugging and improving the performance of machine learning models in large-scale real-world applications. The implementation of the approach is made available as part of a general debugging framework that can be applied to multiple machine learning algorithms, and the framework is accompanied by a user-friendly interface that provides easy access to its key features. The proposed algorithm achieves significant improvements in debugging time, and the results produced by the approach are shown to align closely with those obtained through exhaustive enumeration. The paper also explores the theoretical aspects of computing the Shapley value for training examples and provides a formal definition of the problem, as well as a discussion of the existing connections between the problem and other related areas, such as the computation of the Shapley value in cooperative game theory and the development of efficient algorithms for computing the value of a game. Additionally, our findings in globular clusters may be relevant to understanding the dynamics of nuclear star clusters at the hearts of galaxies.

Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, the spreading of the entangled wave function raises the issue of how long it takes for a particle to recognize a change in its entangled counterpart, implying that previous discussions on this topic have been premature. We rectify this by developing a quantum-optical representation of the Stern-Gerlach experiment, which facilitates the exploration of this concern through the application of scattering matrix and input-output operator forms. Although the spread of the entangled wave function appears to be infinite in this representation, our findings suggest that it is actually limited by the group velocity of light, offering a minimum timeframe of approximately nanoseconds for a particle to discern a change in its counterpart. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the non-local properties associated with single-particle entanglement, enabling the exploration of its practical implementations. In addition, it sheds light on longstanding debates regarding the propagation of single-particle entanglement and its connection to the wave function's collapse. Furthermore, we propose a novel approach to implementing truly non-local tasks by combining single-particle entanglement with quantum non-demolition measurements, offering a potential solution to overcome the issue of decoherence posing a significant barrier to such endeavors. In our proposal, we outline a protocol for rejuvenating the entangled wave function through repeated quantum non-demolition measurements, which facilitates the exploration of this concern through the application of scattering matrix and input-output operator forms.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to reduced data exchange. Simulation results demonstrate the proposed approach offers superior performance over traditional methods in terms of spectral efficiency and reduced feedback information, with small performance losses due to reduced codebook size. Furthermore, large-scale GMM applications are also explored. Overall, the proposed approach yields enhanced performance, efficiency, and complexity across 4G and 5G systems. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability. Our findings show that the proposed method can effectively produce safe pathways for our connected vehicle throughout the traffic light phases. Additionally, we analyze the impact of varying tuning parameters on the controller's effectiveness. A key advantage of our approach is that it minimizes reliance on detailed driver modeling, instead leveraging real-world data to predict the behavior of human drivers. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation speed of nearly three orders of magnitude, reaching approximately one million actions per second on a single CPU core. TextWorldExpress maintains comparable difficulty and rules to its original counterparts while introducing several innovations that enhance gameplay realism and make the games more user-friendly. On top of that, we've developed a unified framework for integrating multiple CPU cores and various virtual machine environments to further maximize simulation efficiency. TextWorldExpress is released with a range of evaluation metrics and testing protocols to facilitate fair comparison of different text-based game simulations. Our research showcases the potential of text-based games to support the rigorous testing of virtual agents in tasks involving natural language understanding. Furthermore, the research highlights the value of open-source text-based games with high performance standards in areas like artificial intelligence research, providing accessible platforms for experimenting with cutting-edge technologies. TextWorldExpress is made available over Stable Baselines' online interface, making it easy to integrate our challenging text games with the latest artificial intelligence algorithms. Our research is also accompanied by a research paper that's been accepted for presentation at the 2019 Conference of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence. TextWorldExpress is an open-source project with a GitHub repository that's freely accessible to the public. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed that reduces memory requirements by up to 75% compared to the standard LSTM. To further minimize memory usage without sacrificing computational capacity, an alternative model called FDHT-LSTM2 is created that employs previously computed output values to facilitate shared memory utilization. In conjunction with this optimized algorithm, a custom hardware platform called FDHT-LSTM-HW is designed to support the efficient execution of these compressed LSTM models, leveraging the hierarchical capabilities of the tensor decomposed data to accelerate data loading and computation by up to 3.3 times. Experimental results indicate that the proposed FDHT-LSTM2 model exhibits comparable accuracy to the standard LSTM while achieving significant memory savings, and can be executed at a high frequency on the custom hardware platform, resulting in a notable increase in performance without incurring a energy efficiency cost. In addition to its practical applications, the relatively small size of the FDHT-LSTM2 model also makes it more suitable for deployment on mobile devices. In comparison to existing compressed LSTM models that primarily focus on weight compression, the FDHT-LSTM2 model offers enhanced computational capacity and data loading acceleration, leading to its superior performance in video recognition tasks. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM2 model provides a balance between algorithmic innovation and hardware integration, serving as a model example for the tensor decomposed algorithm and hardware co-design methodology. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies conducted at high pressures of oxygen reveal that V$_2$O$_3$ films formed on titanium dioxide buffersubstrates undergo a metal-insulator transition induced by monoclinic-lanthanoid structural changes despite being just atomic layers thick but the effectiveness of this transition is heavily influenced by the surface termination. It is observed that films terminated with V-O surfaces exhibit large resistivity jumps greater than tenfold in comparison to oxided terminated films which only show resistivity increases by a factor of roughly three. Notably, the resistance of V-O terminated films closely follows the resistance of bulk V$_2$O$_3$ but the oxided terminated films exhibit different behavior. This distinction in resistance for oxided and v-o surfaces of V$_2$O$_3$ is attributed to variations in the electronic properties of these surfaces which result from different arrangements of surface atoms.  This discovery has the potential to impact the interpretation of data from earlier studies of V$_2$O$_3$ conducted at the surface or with surface-sensitive techniques like photoemission.  It also highlights the difficulty of accurately modeling the effects of bulk and surface doping without consideration of the impact on such arrangements of surface atoms.  Further, it may provide a basis for examining the metal-insulator transition in other systems with complex surface chemistry.  Ultimately, it may be essential to account for the effect of surface termination along with other factors like strain, doping and adsorbates in the discussion of sufficient conditions for an itinerant metal-insulator transition.  This effect should be a consideration for any future theoretical models in the field. Unlike traditional methods, our approach leverages a hybrid-treatment for fractures to enhance numerical accuracy and flexibility. Within each subdomain, we employ a mixed finite element method utilizing $H(\text{div};\Omega)$ and $H^1(\Omega)$ spaces to solve the partial differential equations. For persistent fractures, our approach involves solving reduced interface problems, while for branch-like fractures, we implement constraint equations derived from fracture extensions. This hybrid approach allows for non-matching meshes in the matrix and fracture domains, providing numerical solutions with high accuracy and flexibility in modeling complex fractures. Our proposed method displays convergence in $L^2$ norm, and we provide a priori error estimates for both types of fractures. This approach can be adapted for use in computational models, including those involving multiple fractures and permeability variations. Our results demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency on a range of test cases, including examples with persistent fractures, branch-like fractures, and combinations of both. We examine the conductance of a spin-valve setup that contains a single magnetic layer with a spiral structure, surrounded by superconducting layers. Our analysis shows that the spiral magnetic layer divides into distinct domains with unique magnetic properties, influencing the conductance when a perpendicular external magnetic field is applied. This response is closely related to the anisotropy of superconducting layers, which can originate from the misalignment of magnetic fields between the spiral layer and the superconducting layers. Our research identifies specific conditions under the presence of proximity effects, where the spiral layer's spin-valve behavior can be isolated, allowing for the maximization of the conductance difference when an external magnetic field is varied. This optimal scenario is characterized by a significant conductance gap when the spiral layer's domain is aligned with the superconducting layers' spins. We further explore how this phenomenon is modulated by the spiral layer's magnetic field, revealing that the optimal conditions can be shifted to yield maximal conductance at the spiral layer's ferromagnetic state. This involves the layer's domain being aligned with the superconducting layers' spins, and results in an opposite conductance pattern. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the intricate workings of a single spiral magnetic layer-based spin-valve setup, offering avenues for its experimental verification and potential applications in highly sensitive magnetic field detectors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this type of spin-valve setup can serve as an ideal component for a long-range magnetic field-sensing device, capable of detecting spiral magnetic patterns over extensive distances. Our analysis also extends to magnetization patterns formed in response to local electrical injections, enabling the design of advanced magnetic data storage systems with enhanced security against magnetic field tampering. Lastly, our research can be adapted for the exploration of exotic magnetic phenomena in quantum simulations, where the spiral layer's spin-valve behavior can be modulated through controlled applications of external magnetic fields and electrical injections. Our study provides a theoretical framework for the design of intricate magnetic systems, enabling the precise engineering of their magnetic properties, and sheds light on the underlying mechanisms governing the conductance of a single spiral magnetic layer-based spin-valve setup. Furthermore, our research can be applied to develop strategies for the experimental detection of controlled quantum coherences and controlled quantum state manipulation in quantum simulations. To understand the role these indicators play in sentence semantics, we develop a semantic analysis tool for sentence pairs, leveraging a pre-existing discourse-specific taxonomy. Specifically, we utilize a taxonomic system that categorizes discourse indicators by the type of inference they imply, which is then used to extend the scope of inference to the entire sentence pair. Our approach incorporates a set of predefined relationships between the indicators, the parent-taxonomic categories they belong to, and the semantic representation of each sentence in the pair. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we create a variety of complex sentence combinations and show that our approach accurately identifies the implied discourse indicator and the underlying inference. Furthermore, our technique enables the incorporation of discourse indicators in a range of reasoning tasks about sentence meaning, including the detection of inconsistent or contradictory statements. The implementation of our method allows for both sequential and parallel processing of sentence pairs, with the latter resulting in significantly faster computation. Additionally, we explore multiple techniques for combining the semantic representations of sentence pairs, in addition to our default approach based on the taxonomic structure of the discourse indicators. The development of a discourse analysis tool like DiscSense has several potential applications, including the enhancement of artificial intelligence systems with more sophisticated semantic understanding and the detection of stylistic variations in writing, such as those found in literary works. The tool also provides valuable insights for the field of natural language processing, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive taxonomy of discourse indicators that can facilitate the analysis of multiple types of inferences. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  This value, obtained through analysis of the nonradiative decay rates at high temperatures, supports the idea that a large energy barrier plays a crucial role in the nitrogen-vacancy center's behavior at high temperatures.  Furthermore, we observed that temperature has a substantial impact on the nitrogen-vacancy center's optical transitions, far exceeding its effect on magnetic resonance transitions.  This knowledge is valuable for optimizing the performance of diamond-based quantum technologies under high-temperature conditions.  Additionally, we explored the nitrogen-vacancy center's properties when surrounded by air at high temperatures and found that its radiative decay rate is significantly increased, likely due to the presence of oxygen, which causes a perceived shortening of the radiative decay time.  This effect, however, does not align with our previous findings under vacuum conditions, suggesting the need for further research into the nitrogen-vacancy center's interactions with its surroundings at high temperatures.  This study provides valuable insights into the nitrogen-vacancy center's behavior when subjected to high temperatures and may facilitate the development of more resilient quantum technologies.  This work also highlights the importance of thoroughly characterizing diamond samples, which can exhibit varying temperatures despite controlled environmental conditions, as demonstrated by temperature gradients visible in our optical spectroscopy data.  To ensure accurate results, it is essential to incorporate temperature gradients into any data analysis.  This is particularly significant in temperature-sensitive applications utilizing diamond, as even small deviations can result in inaccuracies of at least 10 percent.  To further optimize these systems, it is recommended that future research focus on mitigating the effects of temperature gradients, as well as exploring ways to minimize the nitrogen-vacancy center's decay rate at high temperatures, which currently constrains its operational lifespan to under an hour when temperature gradients are present.
