Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Furthermore, the representation of GCNN layers as matched filters facilitates the comparison with traditional CNNs, thereby shedding light on the reasons behind GCNNs' ability to effectively learn node representations in graph domains. The paper concludes by examining potential future research directions for GCNNs, considering issues related to data efficiency, the exploration of different activation functions, and the potential risks involved in the overfitting of nodes with distinct characteristics. The text also includes a comprehensive glossary to standardize the notation used throughout the paper, especially in regards to terms related to neural networks and signal processing. The exploration of GCNNs is further illustrated through the application of these networks to the retrieval of seismic data, presenting both numerical and graphical examples along the way. The paper is primarily aimed at experts in neural networks and signal processing; the introduction to matched filtering and the analysis of GCNN layers will also be useful to graduate students in these fields. The discussion on GCNNs is equally relevant to the broader community working with neural networks in the time-domain. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Additionally, a comparison with the conventional beamforming technique, side-fire configuration, reveals the VSSA technique's displacements are 137% more accurate and feature lower standard deviations. The research indicates that VSSA outperforms side-fire configuration, suggesting its potential as an advanced imaging technique for the accurate estimation of mechanical properties in ultrasound elastography. This technique's precise lateral displacement estimation may enhance the detection of soft tissue abnormalities and contribute significantly to medical diagnostics. Furthermore, its high performance resolution can facilitate the sensitive detection of various pathological conditions, such as cancer, cardiovascular, and kidney diseases. This study's findings can serve as a foundation for the development of more advanced ultrasound elastography techniques, as well as its application in medical sonography education and clinical practice. Additionally, this study's outcomes can be used to evaluate and compare existing and novel ultrasound elastography techniques. This study's novel virtual source synthetic aperture technique, capable of delivering high lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, may also be integrated with other advanced ultrasound techniques, such as contrast-enhanced ultrasound, shockwave therapy, and ultrasound-guided interventions, to enhance their performance. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This new framework is illustrated through examples, including solutions to reachability problems and the resolution of type systems. The development of logical pseudocodes offers a novel demonstration of the algebraic theory of secure logical functional programming, showcasing its practical applicability. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the exploration of additional properties of programs by combining forward and backward reasoning within the framework. This has implications for both the theoretical study of computability logic and its potential real-world applications. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that our algorithm's coreset accurately minimizes the $k$-means distance to a target set within a factor of approximately $\Delta$ when considering the optimal solution, and approximately $1$ when considering the optimal solution that assigns the same weight to all points. Building upon this foundation, we also design a two-pass $O(k^2)$-storage algorithm that significantly reduces the memory requirement. This is achieved by initially utilizing a variant of our one-pass algorithm to generate an intermediate coreset, followed by a second pass that leverages this coreset to solve the $k$-means clustering problem. Lastly, we also investigate the feasibility of $o(k)$-dimension-dependent storage in our one-pass algorithm, demonstrating that any algorithm requiring less than $d$ dimensions' worth of storage would imply the existence of a $2$-pass algorithm employing less than $2k$ dimensions' worth of storage, thus indicating that such algorithms are likely optimal. This serves as a novel storage lower bound for dynamic $k$-means clustering. We investigate a type of stochastic game called pursuit-evasion, where a group of leaders move freely, while a group of followers with known locations must be captured. The leaders' objectives are to minimize the number of captures, while the followers aim to increase the number of captures. The complexity of these games arises from the underlying worm-like structure and the randomness of the spaces used. We divide the structure into a hierarchy of connected regions and solve the game for each part individually. By combining these solutions, we get a strategy for the entire game. Although no general method exists for solving complex pursuit-evasion games, our hierarchy provides an efficient way to tackle games with numerous random events. It does this by limiting the number of possible state changes in each individual part, making it feasible to apply randomized methods. We test and compare different approaches to the games by changing the randomness and the layout of the structure. Our studies show that the efficiency of our hierarchical method can be quite high, often close to the best performance of more general methods. We also explore how the performance of the games could be affected if the followers move further away from the leaders. Finally, we apply our hierarchical approach to a real-world scenario involving the capture of sea lions. Our research could also be used to model and solve other complex games, such as those involving the capture of targets in networks. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values for $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating that the probability of choosing a 'cyclic' n-tuple increases in a manner proportional to $n^{-1}$.

Notably, we demonstrate that the condition of all individual elements $x_i$ being greater than 0.5 is unnecessary for an n-tuple to be considered 'cyclic', and we explore how the associated distribution of likelihoods $x_i$ impacts 'nontransitive' behavior. Furthermore, we establish that both 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' phenomena can be applied broadly across various domains by presenting corresponding examples in the context of preference, preference differences, differences in opinion, opinion, growth rates, and rate of growth. Lastly, we examine potential avenues for extension to negative range values and probabilities outside the [0,1] interval. Additionally, we provide an informal discussion on the related concepts of counterfactuals and the surprising nature of the results. Finally, we outline potential directions for further research on upper and lower limits for $p_n^*$. system\.abstract$

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single adapter network, where we employ adapter modules in the encoder and decoder of the mapping networks, allowing for efficient training without the need for extra memory. By leveraging the cycle consistency constraint and identity mappings, our model achieves a high level of accuracy in enhancing low-dose CT images without the need for matching high-dose images, outperforming previous cycleGAN-based methods while requiring significantly less memory. Experimental results on a CT dataset show that our proposed model matches the quality of non-DeepLearning denoising methods, specifically ANLS and BM3D, while demonstrating particular improvement in noisy regions. Furthermore, our model exhibits a significant reduction in training time and memory usage. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing similar dialogs to be identical which hinders the discovery of fundamental dialog structures. To address this limitation, this research introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured semi-supervised pre-trained model that extracts basic dialog elements and their relationships. It combines two contrastive learning objectives: a semi-supervised objective that treats dialog samples with different turns as similar, and a structural objective that treats dialog turns with the same role as similar, allowing the model to capture fundamental dialog structures. Experimental results show that SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance on various dialog understanding tasks in CLOTH and MultiWOZ datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/zheng-xy/S4TD. With the code, we also conduct thorough ablation studies and additional experiments to analyze the effect of different dialog structure patterns on the performance of dialog understanding tasks. Our research indicates that models pre-trained with the proposed SPACE-2 method can effectively capture the structures of dialog texts, extracting crucial elements and their meaningful interactions, ultimately enhancing performance on dialog understanding tasks. The pre-trained models can also be fine-tuned with minimal labeled data for optimal performance on real-world tasks, providing a solution to the dataset imbalance issue. The results of our experiments demonstrate that SPACE-2 delivers superior performance to baseline models on various dialog understanding tasks in the CLOTH and MultiWOZ datasets. The proposed method offers a more flexible framework for pre-training dialog understanding models on text than baseline methods, allowing the extraction of fundamental dialog element structures for better performance on real-world tasks. To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states and remain intact under rotation, except for $^{44}$Mg where shape decoupling occurs. Due to the rising interest in muon colliders as future high-energy particle accelerators, it is essential to analyze W and Z boson production across a broad range of energy levels, spanning from their creation thresholds up to energies near those reached in proposed future facilities. Despite being heavily produced, these bosons are often used as energy calibration tools, meaning their properties must be accurately understood, especially when they are highly energetic. To this end, we utilize QCD formalisms to examine the kinematic characteristics of muons and electrons emitted from W and Z boson decays, particularly when these particles are highly energetic. The parameters of this straight-line approximation are provided for their energies, momentum components, and helicity states. It is also shown that when considering highly energetic muon collisions, the decays of W and Z bosons can be treated as if they were isolated, a fact with significant implications for muon collider physics. A unified framework is presented, leveraging theorems about the limits of formal languages to derive these significant results with minimal assumptions about the formal system in question. Additionally, our analysis yields novel consequences and extensions of the aforementioned results, including a broader undefinability theorem and a Godelian pair generation method. These results are then applied to demonstrate the limits of extensions of a formal system and its associated provability function, followed by an examination of the definitional capacity of reflection principles along these lines. A primary focus is given to exploring the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of these results within the realm of recursively enumerable theories. Lastly, we explore extending these results to beyond the realm of computability theory. A key component of our presentation is the use of modern formal systems to recast classic incompleteness theorems and to clarify the connection between the syntactic derivation of these results and the fundamental properties of computability. This approach provides a more intuitive understanding of the underlying computations involved in the derivation of these theorems. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for a broader theory of the limits of formal languages, encompassing both the limits of computability and those of uncomputability. Traditionally, large distances between the transmitter and receiver in some applications have necessitated the use of relay nodes to facilitate communication. An important step in THz wireless networks is beam training, which allows the transmitter and receiver to identify optimal directions for data transfer. However, this process is highly time-consuming and demands the development of more efficient methods, especially in multi-hop THz networks where the transmitter must train its beam with the aid of multiple relay nodes. We present a novel approach to optimize beam training in these networks by utilizing a method called deep deterministic policy gradient. This approach first simulates the THz propagation characteristics, including the limited communication distance and high error rates, by generating a subset of reliable relay nodes from which the transmitter can communicate. We then develop a multi-agent system to represent the transmitter and the most reliable relay nodes and design a deep neural network to predict the best transmit and receive directions. The performance of this proposed method is compared to existing techniques by conducting numerical studies, revealing significant improvements in network throughput and a marked increase in the effective communication distance. The optimal deep neural network can also be adapted to accommodate changing network conditions, thereby enabling efficient beam training in multi-hop THz networks. Experimental validation of our findings is also presented by conducting a range of simulations. Analytical and numerical results are validated against actual THz network measurements, and the code for the proposed scheme is provided, demonstrating the feasibility of our approach by successfully transferring data at a rate of up to 2 Gb/s in a real-world THz network. Overall, our optimized beam training method significantly reduces training time by as much as 75%, a crucial breakthrough for the practical implementation of THz communication technology. We also explore the potential for our proposed method to be applied to other frequency bands and examine the limitations and potential applications of our approach, in addition to identifying avenues for further research into the optimization of THz communication systems. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Multiple screens contribute to scintillation patterns throughout the pulsar's rotation period, allowing for their identification and characterization. Based on these screens and their sizes, a large one was found with an unusually long timescale of about 30 years, likely composed of smaller screens or a screen with a large scale height. This large screen is likely the outer boundary of a structure including the Local Interstellar Cloud and the G-Cloud. Models of the scintillations also revealed a small screen breaking into fragments, possibly related to the entering Solar wind, and evidence of two other possible screens with unclear origins. These findings highlight the value of prolonged pulsar observations in understanding the interstellar medium. Additionally, this research demonstrates how screens can be confirmed and their properties refined through the analysis of dynamic spectra and scintillation patterns. This approach is particularly useful for studying the interstellar medium through the observation of bright pulsars with minimal receiver bandwidth. This can result in the discovery of screens and their properties, as well as potential transverse components of screen velocities. This technique is also an effective use of archival and future radio pulsar data, especially with the ever-advancing sensitivity of radio telescopes. This paper's methods and findings are relevant to ongoing and upcoming pulsar and scintillation studies with more sensitive and wide-band receivers, such as those with the Square Kilometre Array. Therefore, this research is a significant step in the ongoing pursuit of understanding the Local Interstellar Medium and the interstellar medium as a whole. This knowledge is essential in addressing questions about the structure and composition of the interstellar medium, the formation of stars and planetary systems within it, and the impact of this environment on nearby stars and the Sun itself. This research is also a foundation for future studies of the interstellar medium using pulsar scintillation, including the potential for the detection of magnetic fields within the interstellar medium, the velocity of screen components, and the three-dimensional structure of screens, as well as the search for other screens and structures within the interstellar medium. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. The project's code is available at https://github.com/zhengdeng-dai/LGCN. The paper's findings are also visually illustrated in an interactive 3D visualization video available at https://youtu.be/9f6vB2FZDUU. Furthermore, a comparison with existing hyperbolic GCNs that fail to adhere to hyperbolic geometry geometry, namely HGCN and MT3, reveals that these networks may learn node features that are, in fact, embedded in Euclidean space, and in some cases, they even outperform LGCN on certain datasets, highlighting the importance of rigorous geometric analysis in the design of graph convolutional networks. Additionally, an investigation into the effects of distortion in graph data is also conducted, along with a discussion on future research directions for non-Euclidean GCNs. This research is a step towards developing more effective and robust graph convolutional networks that can handle complex, real-world graph data by incorporating fundamental geometric principles. It is anticipated that this work will contribute to a deeper understanding of graph data and the design of more powerful machine learning models. Furthermore, this research has the potential to be expanded to other non-Euclidean geometries, such as spherical and projective geometries, and it is crucial to explore these extensions in future research. The field of graph convolutional networks in non-Euclidean geometry is still in its nascent stages, and there are numerous avenues for future research to be uncovered.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, obtained from a global uniqueness result in the case of an isolated obstacle, indicating that the structural acoustic wave system acts as a global identifier for the source term. Notably, the stability estimate yields a precise formula for the optimal regularity of the solution. Additionally, this research demonstrates the efficacy of hybrid functional approach variants in resolving the inverse problem. Specifically, it leverages the Helmholtz decomposition to divide the source term into potential and solenoidal components, both of which can be recovered through separate Carleman estimate-based estimates. This division enables the extension of the approach to non-isotropic structures. Furthermore, this study extends the method to non-isotropic structures, such as ellipsoidal obstacles, for which it provides a more general uniqueness framework and a stability estimate, as well as a uniqueness framework and a stability estimate for the potential and solenoidal source terms. Lastly, this research is complemented by numerical experiments illustrating its practical applications. The experiments involve the reconstruction of a acoustic scattering model consisting of an isolated spherical obstacle with varying curvature and a plane obstacle with a curved edge. The results show excellent agreement with theoretical stability estimates, and highlight the method's ability to recover both potential and solenoidal source terms using a flexible variant of the least squares approach. The method's flexibility enables the exploration of alternative formulations, such as the conventional least squares formulation and the regularized formulation. The former yields a more robust solution, while the latter yields a solution with better consistency with the theoretical stability estimate. The study also examines how the choice of regularization parameter affects the solution, and demonstrates the method's ability to recover source terms in the case of wave equations modeling seismic acoustic wave propagation in oceans. The results demonstrate the method's potential for the reconstruction of acoustic scattering models in applications such as seismac acoustic wave inversion, with potential applications to the imaging of ocean bottoms and subsurfaces. The study provides a detailed analysis of the method's convergence properties, and the effects of variations in the method's parameters on the solution, as well as a discussion of potential extensions to the method, such as its extension to the inversion of seismic travel

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This model is found to be equivalent to the linearized version of dRGT massive gravity.  We also demonstrate that all harmonic gauges lead to massive linearized gravity models with the correct number of degrees of freedom, although they differ in their predictions for gravitational wave polarization states.  This provides a gauge theory explanation for the distinct predictions made by different massive gravity models.  We further observe that these models exhibit a generalization of the homotopy property first noted by Chiao and Friedman.  Ultimately, our analysis indicates that harmonic gauge theories offer a broader framework for formulating massive gravity models and resolving the issue of massive gravity's degree of freedom count.  However, resolving the problem of radiational stability in massive gravity requires a more comprehensive approach than linearized harmonic gauge theory can provide.  We conclude by outlining an extension of this research that could address this remaining challenge.  This note is a summary of the research presented in arXiv:2103.04330 and arXiv:2107.03162.  We would like to refer the reader to those detailed studies for further information.  Instead, this note is intended to serve as an addendum to arXiv:2107.03162, specifically addressing the additional feedback received from the community since the latter study was submitted.  In response to the raised concerns and questions, we have included the following additional comments.  Firstly, we clarify that the original motivation for investigating harmonic gauge theories originated from the work of Chiao and Friedman, as did the initial awareness of the issue's broader homotopy-related context.  Secondly, we address the question regarding whether a similar analysis could be performed for the Bessel gauge recently discussed in arXiv:1905.00944.  We have demonstrated that the Bessel gauge is not a harmonic gauge.  Consequently, it does not possess the same degree-of-freedom counting characteristics as harmonic gauges do.  Lastly, we outline the results

Homeomorphism in signed graphs is equivalent to homeomorphism in regular graphs, but other types of homomorphisms behave differently. This paper investigates the minimum number of signs required to satisfy the inequality $|a_1| + \cdots + |a_g| \geq k$ for all elements $a_i \in G$, where it is also considered what group sizes $G$ could potentially reach the given inequality $|a_1| + \cdots + |a_g| \geq k$ with exactly $t$ positive signs. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. To foster collaboration, we present a initial prototype for the semi-automated annotation of dysplasia and carcinoma, enabling researchers to efficiently expand the dataset based on expert pathologists' assessments. UniToPatho's annotation guidelines and the developed dataset are currently being utilized in a related competition at the MICCAI 2021 grand challenge. The annotation protocol, dataset, and source code are made publicly available to contribute to the advancement of computational pathology. UniToPatho has been co-created in collaboration with pathologists from the University of Zurich and the University of Bern. The developed approach and resulting dataset highlights the potential for a collaborative effort between computer scientists and pathologists to accelerate the development of histopathological imaging analysis solutions. The dataset's distinct features, annotation protocol, and developed methodology are expected to contribute positively to the field of computational pathology. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach involves breaking down the solution into an incoming wave and a scattered wave with specific properties, including boundedness and the satisfaction of certain radiation conditions. The key innovation lies in a dynamic boundary condition reformulation which facilitates the representation of inhomogeneities as intersections of tubular elements, each representing the propagation of plane waves in different directions. This reformulation enables the development of an adaptive mesh refinement technique that targets areas where scattering most significantly affects the solution's behavior. This approach results in highly localized refinement, leading to a substantial reduction in unnecessary degrees of freedom and, consequently, a significant improvement in computational efficiency. This efficiency gains are particularly pronounced in scenarios involving smoothly varying large-scale inhomogeneities and could be integrated with existing quasi-analytical approximations for specific configurations. This method has been numerically tested against established results for both smooth and sharp interface cases, showing consistent evidence of improved accuracy and marked reductions in estimated solution degrees of freedom across all test scenarios. This includes simulations of both subwavelength and wavelength-sized scattering objects across a wide range of frequency benchmarks. Furthermore, this approach has demonstrated the potential for further optimization through the use of more efficient but less stable iterative solvers which could yield additional performance benefits. This research provides a foundation for the exploration of more complex scattering scenarios, including those involving smoothly varying boundary surfaces and changes in frequency, both of which hold significant importance in the broader field of acoustic scattering studies. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of D-poor hydrogen was present in the nebula, with the remaining D-rich water contributing 5-55$\%$. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thus circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Furthermore, they prove highly adaptable to new language pairs with just a few-shot dataset, achieving scores of up to 26.1 BLEU points. For instance, on the Switchboard dataset for the English-to-French language pair, a model trained with only 50 samples achieved a score of 21.2 BLEU points. We also explore various model architectures and observe that transformer-based models outperform RNN-based models. Our code and models are available for public perusal. Surprisingly, our zero-shot speech-to-text models perform subpar to baseline speech recognition models. We attribute this underperformance to speech recognition models' propensity to generate similar representations for semantically distinct sentences. As a result, they excel in recognizing similar sentences, including those that aren't text. We experiment with modifying speech recognition models to generate disparate representations for sentences with differing meanings. We employ a contrastive loss function that treats identical spoken text as negative examples and aggregate the gradients to broaden the representations' scope. Our results indicate that these modifications yield zero-shot speech recognition models with lower loss rates and more accurate scores on unseen text. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic scattering and optical force: Mie theory with various multipolar expansions, the T-matrix method, and effective medium approximations. Our analysis shows that full Mie theory, which considers all multipolar contributions, provides the most accurate results. However, its accuracy depends on the wavelength and the specific properties of the particles being considered. While the long wavelength approximation of Mie theory is sufficient for many purposes, it fails to account for the fine details of particle scattering and optical force. In contrast, the T-matrix method offers a detailed analysis of the electromagnetic field within the particle, albeit at the expense of more complex calculations. Furthermore, we find that effective medium approximations are not accurate enough for our high-resolution standards. We also investigate the peculiar behavior of certain particle properties, such as the anomalous dipole moment of a specific octupole mode, which cannot be captured by a simple long wavelength approximation. Building on our analysis, we provide a roadmap for the development of improved effective medium models that take into account the unique properties of particles across different size and composition categories. Such models would enable the rapid calculation of optical force and scattering for various particles, bridges the gap between numerical simulations and analytical models, and facilitates the link between particle characteristics and their response to light. In turn, this would facilitate a deeper understanding of particle behavior and the optimization of material properties for specific applications. In the context of plasmonics, we propose the use of a damped Drude model, which accurately captures the high-frequency regime of particle response and offers a potential pathway for the enhancement of optical force calculations. Ultimately, this work paves the way for a more unified understanding of particle properties, an improved description of particle behavior through analytical models, and a bridge between numerical simulations and such models. Furthermore, it facilitates a deeper understanding of particle characteristics and their response to light, as well as the identification of material properties that could be optimized for specific applications. In the realm of plasmonics, we propose the use of a damped Drude model, which provides a pathway for a more accurate description of optical force and scattering. In the future, this approach can be expanded to consider other phenomena, such as nonlinear optical force and scattering, and could serve as a foundation for the investigation of other collective and coherent effects that occur when particles are excited by light. Using generative adversarial networks, we developed a novel application in medical imaging, where a disease-aware generative model transforms normal images into realistic images mimicking specific pathological conditions, based on annotated segmentation masks, for the purpose of expanding limited datasets or creating artificial training data. Specifically, we trained a conditional generative adversarial network on a large dataset of normal and pneumonia-infected chest X-rays, enabling it to produce high-quality pneumonia-infected images from normal chest X-rays. However, our findings indicate that current models overlook the underlying pathology when generating artificial images, which is attributed to the incomplete nature of semi-supervised annotations. As a result, we discovered that these models are prone to producing over-smoothed images with exaggerated features, which can lead to biased classification outcomes, specifically in scenarios involving few-shot learning. To address these limitations, we explored the use of disease-aware editing tools to add subtle pathological features to normal chest X-rays, which serves as a more complex challenge due to the intricate nature of chest X-ray images, leading to suboptimal results even when achieving visually pleasing outcomes, which raises intriguing research questions regarding the intersection of disease-aware editing, generation, and classification tasks. As such, we introduce a new metric, called semantic quality factor, which gauges the plausible incorporation of pathological features into normal chest X-rays, offering a starting point for further exploration into the intricacies of disease-aware image editing. As the field of medical imaging continues to evolve, our work highlights the significance of delving into the intricacies of generative models through the lens of semantics, as well as the potential applications of transfer learning in expanding limited medical datasets. As such, our disease-aware editing framework serves as a foundational stepping stone for future research aimed at refining the performance of medical imaging models through the efficient generation and editing of high-quality, realistic pathological images. As such, we openly contribute our pre-trained models, along with our experimental results, to the community, which provides valuable insights into the complexities of medical imaging, while also sparking new discussion on the semantics of transfer learning. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this research, we introduce an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, for certain applications such as electrostatics, smooth representations of a function within grid cells are sufficient, which allows us to leverage recent breakthroughs in numerical linear algebra to solve high-order system equations accurately and reliably. In this research, we provide a detailed analysis of our method's convergence properties, as well as concrete numerical examples demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. Furthermore, we explore potential extensions of our method to higher-dimensional domains and discuss the method's relevance to solving volume integral equations using the Helsing-Ojala method. In addition, we make available our implementation of this method in C++ for reference purposes. In particular, we consider the challenge of adapting this method for applications involving non-smooth functions, which poses significant computational barriers. In conclusion, our research offers an influential solution to the long-standing challenge of efficiently computing Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions using grid-based methods.
